MUMM-EkS DECAY. When my first roses shed Their petals, and lay dead, I knew my foe Decay Had struck at my sweet day Of summer breath and bloom. I heard my knell of doom In the soft sighing breeze That scattered their dead leaves. And then and there I seemed To see as one who dreamed A long procession pass Across the spriliginggrass--

Sweet ghost s of bed ad flowers That bloomed in last year's hours. And stately at the head, All clad in white and red, Shedding their dewy scent, My fair June darlings went; And following after stout My lilies, who had kept Their garments white as snow, While their warmehearts did glow With all the golden fire
VW IT .ACTS. HELD DOWN IN BED BY TWO

That summer suns inspire. All blooms and blossoms fair Followed and followed there, ' Until I did behold, White as the stars, and cold, My pale chrysanthemums pass; And then I knew, alas! The end had come; and knew, While still the warm winds blew, My darlings of to-day Like this were on their way To join the ghostly throng; Like this would move along, Pale visions, dead and dear, To haunt another year. Shuddering, I moaned and wept, And in that moment crept Shaddows of storm and night Across my summer light- " What is my summer pride?" Moaning, I wept and cried, "Why do I hold my way. If only to decay?" Then suddenly I heard Amid my boughs a bird Lifting a heavenly voice. " Rejoice, and yet rejoice," He sang; and sang again: '4 Out of this earth-bound pain, Out of this dread decay, I lift my heavenly lay. Higher and higher still, Sweet with a sweeter thrill, Lifted that heavenly song. Borne on its wings along, I saw the bloom and birth Of the new heaven and earth, And all my flowery host, _ , Each sweet departing ghost, Seemed in my ears to sing: "No fair and beauteous thing, Nothing of precious cost, Nothing we love, is lost." —Harper's Magazine.

On Monday evening Sir Gilbert Greenell addressed a meeting of his supporters in Soutb-West Ward at St. Mary's School, Bank Quay, when the chair was occupied by Mr. T. Sutton. In an address in reply to a resolution pledging the meeting to support his candidature, Sir GIL- D/MT GanntraLL referred to the question of the Ship Canal. Re said that he bad thought it his duty to take shares, without any idea of making a profit, but brcause he thought that the expenditure of money that would accrue from the making of the canal would greatly benefit Warrington. Ile had no objection to promise his first ten years' dividend to tke Warrington Infirmary, but, the times being so tickle, it was perhaps scarcely legal for him to make the promise at present.—On Tuesday evening a meeting was held in St. James' Schoolroom, Latchford, under the presidency of Captain Reynolds, and on Thursday evening Mr. P. Stubs presided at a meetieg held in John.street. At both ad- dresses were delivered by the candidate, and resolutions ippon passed.

Eantaerrows v. BOOTLB.—A large crowd of spectators assembled on thelliesnee, Earlestown, on Saturday after- noon to wittiest the match between these two teams, and their hopes ef witnessing a hard-fought and exciting game were not disappointed. The home eleven won the toss and elected to play downhill and against the wind in the first half. G. Hutton started the game for Bootle, and for a short time the play was confined to the Barlestown quarters. The Barlestown backs and half-basks defended well, how- ever, and repulsed the attacks of their opponents. The cupbolders gradually assumed the aggressive, and after , some capital passing by the forwards Holcroft scored amid ' loud cheers, thirteen minutes from the commencement. The Bootle men re-started the game, but the Earlestoniant again secured possession of the leather, and after some further exciting play Holcroft again scored—the spectators loudly cheering the point. The subsequent play was slightly in favour of Earlestown, and shortly before hall-time the cup- helders added two more goals. On the change of ends, Bootle being four goals to the bad, went off with a dash, and Byton-Jones chronicled Bootle's first goal, a few minutes 1 from the kick-off. Barlestown retaliated, the ball, from a splendid shot by Ellison, goin4 between Jackson's legs. Bootle then pressed the home team, and scored two goals. Marlestown afterwards scored once, and Bootle did likewise. Shortly before time Earlestowa registered another goal, and when time was called they had won a splendidly-contested and exciting game be seven goals,to four. For the home team the backs and half-backs played a good game, whilst the forward, also distinguished themselves, Bootle played a capital game, Galbraith and the two Buttons being noticeable. Manningham, who were the runners up last season for the Yorkshire Challenge Cup, paid a 'visit to Lower Broughton to play off their fixture with Broughton Bangers. Considerable interest was taken is the game, but unfortu- nately for the Rangers, they were without noggin, Turner, Seddon, and Robertson, and therefore were easily beaten by two tries and five mloors,.againet three miners scored by the Rangers. _ _

Br-ougbton fairly made rings round the Free Wanderers, winning by three- goals, two tries, and fear minors to nothing. Neither team was fully represented. As I anticipated last week, the meeting of North and South Lancashire at Barrow, proved an easy victory for the South, which won by one goal, four Mee, and one minor to one minor point. .

A pleassn't game was that p!ayed en the Warrington ground between that club and Liverpool Gymnasium, the match being witnessed by nearly 2,000 people, who were treated to a tine game, whish was woe by the hems team by one goal (dropped by Barnes) and eight minors to ono minor.

The Runoorn men showed Slashley what they can do on the football field, defeating them te the tuse of two goals, three tries, and three minors to nil. I am told that the game was not near so one sided as the result would give one to understand.

St. Helens are showing now a little of their last year's form, as they fairly covered the colours of the Lymm club. by Sve goals, four tries, and six minors to nothing. Lymtn must have had a merry time of it. The defeat of Widnee by Salford, by two goals, one try, and four minors to three minors, was MHO than the Chemicals expected, but better luck next time. Pam the ball more, Curley The stick and whistle rule, which came into fores last week, will, I fancy, ere long become very popular.

div.head: PRESCOT.
div.p: PRESCOT.

ANIMAL BIEBT2NO AT THB CONCHUMATIONAL CHURCH.— On Thursday week the church and congregation met at the schoolroom, Warrington-road, where tea was provided from 8-30 to 7-30, served by several ladies belonging to the Church. After tea the pastor, the Rev. J. Johnstone, took the chair, and addressed these present generally on the work of the past year. Mr. Haigh followed by reading the annual report, and I. M. Lyon oubmitted the financial statement. Mr. kownall gave the result and explained the working of the weekly offering system since its adoption three years ago, and stated that though there was a alight deficiency in the amount required it was expected it would be made up before the end of the year. Mr. W. Goldeworth, jun., submitted the account of the building fund, which showed, after meet- ing all the expenses recently incurred, tbat there remained a small balance in hand. Mr. Edmund Wright sent a vary Interesting report of the Holt Mission, read by Mr. Forman, which showed a *ery satisfactory result of their labour. A Band of Hope was commenced in connection with the Sunday school on Monday evening and names were en- rolled.

PRRSCOT BOARD OF Guartntaws.—The fortnightly meet- ing was held on Thursday at the Workhouse. Whistonpnear Prescot. Mr. J. Leatherbarrow presided.—The Master re- ported that there were 449 inmates this week, against 451 last week, and 438nin the corresponding period of last year. Vagrants relieved, 36, against 72 in the corresponding period of last year.—The Rev. Father Finegan, of Widnes, moved the following resolution, of which he had given notice That in consideration of the services rendered to. the Roman Catholic inmates of the Wothhouse of this union by the Rev. W. B. Winkler, of Portico, there be made to him during the pleasure of the Board payment at the rate of £75 per annum, as and from the 18th inst." Father Fine- gan stated that half the number of inmates were Catholics, and when it was considered that about 100 of that number were in the hospital, they would at once see that a'large amount of work devolved upon the rev, gentleman and his coadjutors at Portico. He did not think any guardian could say that the amount was excessive, and It was perfectly legal, as shown by the teat case taken UP last year by the Liverpool authorities at Brownlow-hill. Mr. Newsome seconded the resolution, and complimented the Rev. T. Finegan upon the fair way he had placed the matter before the Board.—The Rev. Thomas Chambers (Halewood) said, taking the high ground of Christian charity, fair play, and justice between man and man—and everybody that knew him knew that he was perhaps as far removed as it was possible to be from many practices of the Roman Catholic faith—when he saw members en that Board who were Catholics. and knew that in the Union there were large numbers of Catholic ratepayers, be considered they were equally justified in paying a Roman Catholic instruc- tor as a Church of England clergyman. (Hear, hear.) He supported the resolution, as did also Mr. William Tyrer. The resolution was carried. No hands were held up in op- position, though several guardians did not vote.

div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING.
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING.

THB BEST STOCK s'ent Tin PHAR.—" Gardening World," in its comments on the Pear Show at Chiswick, states that "as regards stocks it is worthy of note that quite three-parts of the samples shown come from trees worked on the Quince; but a comparison of specimens In different collections shows that most of the leading sorts come off equally good quality worked on the Pear stock, whatever may be the difference as regards yield. Another fact which is well brought out, is that the finest samples, almost without exception, are obtained from cordon-trained trees." We have seen trees trained in this fashion so loaded with fruit that they looked like ropes of onions, and we highly commend the system to the notice of all who wish Per variety in a limited space of either apples or pears. The trees may be bought from a shilling apiece upwards, according to sorts and strength of plants. They are occasionally trained on either side of the walks and only a foot or so above the soil. We, however, should prefer nailing them against a wall or secure them to stakes similar to raspbernes, and for this mode we would select the single cordon, which we were informed by one grower, who showed fifty varieties, was the method he adopted. We observed in his collection such choice varieties as Pitmaston Duchess, Gansel's Bergamot, Duchess d'Angouleme, Glou Dforceau, Marie Louise, Beurre Bachelier, Winter Nelis, Beurre Bose, Beurre d'Amaulis, Louise Bonne of Jersey, Ne Plus Meuris, and Easter Beurre; all of which will suc- ceed more or less in most Lancashire gardens if provided with a sunny aspect. Cialuir.—We are now earthing this up for the last time this season, as we feel sure it has now completed its growth. To protect it from frost we bank it well up, and we hope the best will be fit for use as late as March. The earlier crops have done well and are in fine form, but the drought interrupted the growth of late planted ones, and they are not so good as usual. This time of the year, and especially this season, the soil is so wet that it is impossible to proceed with the work of earth- ing up so speedily as in summer, and we first of all pack all the dry soil available next to the plants and the wet round that, which after two or three fine days, through being elevated, becomes in fair condition for additional packing if required. CAIILIFLOWBAS are still forming nice heads, and if it comes frosty it will be necessary to protect them. For the first night or two a few of their own leaves bent over them will suffice, but to protect them from a prolonged frost we find it necessary to place a handful of dry litter over the hearts of all that are, likely to form heads be- tween now and Christmas.

Tan FRONT GARDHN.—The Grass Plot: Some people have a habit of leaving the patch of grass in front of their dwellings totally uncared for towards the end of the season, so that it has a shaggy appearance all through the winter, and when it comes to be cut in spring it is a most difficult task, and when completed reveals patches of bare soil, the clover and weaker grasses having been destroyed—the outcome of ignorance or neglect on the part of the owner. If the grass is cut short now it will require no further attention before the spring,beyond an occasional beating with the back of the spade to ob- literate the worm casts and solidify the sward. Frequent walking over the grass in wet weather, or indeed any kind of weather, in winter acts adversely to its welfare, and it is well known to gardeners that a walk across the lawn on a frosty morning will result in every foot- mark being perfectly black when thaw takes place. The rigid blades refuse to yield to the foot till they are bruised and broken by the pressure; hence the blackened surface. The mild moist "weather has tempted us to move some clumps of herbaceous plants that were en- croaching od their weaker neighbours. Though it is not the orthodox season for conducting such operations in connection with this class of plants, we at the same time feel sure that it will prove successful in the case of vigorous growing plants. Weaker plants are no doubt safer to move at the end of March or during April, but that is a very busy season, and if the whole of the moving business is left till then, some would have to be left undone. Notes should now be made of all plants that have the appearance of being crowded, as a more accurate idea can be formed of the extra space required now that the tops are still on the plants. After all future arrangements are mentally completed, then all decayed leaves and dead stalks should be cleared away and the surface of the ground•made as neat as possible. THE Wilanow.—Hyacinths in water: The cultivation of the hyacinth in glasses containing water supplies an agreeable pastime to all whose duties confine them in- doors. The single varieties are more generally used for this purpose. If two or three lumps of charcoal are put in the water it will prevent its becoming putrid. Fill the glass with water till it almost touches the base of the bulb, and move them afterwards into a cool, dry, dark place, where they may remain for a month or more, till the roots nearly touch the bottom of the glass, when they may be brought out and gradually exposed to more light and air.

' A remarkable demonstration in support of the .candidature of Colonel McCorguodale was witnessed at Haydock on Wednesday night, when the Liberal Oendidate had beet, announced to address a meeting in the Colliery Schools, ldriclty lent for the occasioa by Messrs. Richard Evans and Co. This was the first visit of Colonel McCorpiuodale to Haydock in connection with his political campaign, and the spontaneous enthusiasm of the miners in his favour augurs well forthis slleCesB at the polling booths. Long before thestime announced for the commence- ment of the meeting the people were astir, and the village soon had an animated appearance. The Haydock-Brass Band turned out to welcome Colonel MeCorguodale,!and as the latter was slowly driven through the village he was followed by a large crowd, who lustily cheered along the road. When the sehoolrogra was reached it was found that the room was packed with an earnest and enthusiastic audience—alriost entirely composed of the working classes. Printed copies of popular Liberal songs had been distributed among those present, and Mr. Alfred Sims fed the audience in singing "March, boys, •March." A oumour had been spread through- out the town thatan organised mob intended to disturb the meeting, and there was certainly an appearance of this. WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The usual fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday morning. There were pre- sent—the Rev. G. F. Roberts (chairman), Messrs. Greening, Blackhurst, Jolley, Brown, Appleton, Gibson, Ratcliffe, Humphries, Darbyshire, Jno. Houghton, Wm. Houghton, Harrison, and J. C. Sutton (clerk).

THE WORKHOUSE OVERCROWDED. The House Committee stated in its minutes that the Workkeuse Master reported that the female side of the Work- house had become so full that two women occupied one bed.—Mr. GREENING. in moving the adoption of the min- utes, said that it was contrary to the consolidated order to have two persons in one bed, but the master said this could not be done without. Since Friday there had been five more persons received into the house, and there were 85 more to- day than at this time last year.—Mr. BLACKHURST said they bad before had considerably more people in the Work. house than there were at present. The house, be thought, was sufficiently large for accommodating a great many more. AU that was wanted was a re-arrangement, and not any structural alteration.—Mr. GREENINO said the com- mittee had never suggested any structural alterations.—The Citentuan thought the Board would meet the case if it directed the House Committee to see what could be done and then report to the Bcard.—The CLERK said that if the I numbers of the inmates went on increasing they would have to give up the boardroom temporarily for the use of the in- mates.—The CHAIRMAN said the rchools at Padgate were I alsp full, there being 189 inmates, the accommodation being for 290.—The minutes were then pasted.

_ THE PADMATE SCHOOLS. The Schools Committee reported that Mr. Stephens, the Local Government Board inspector, was present at their meeting and made a suggestion for the better conduct ef prayers which, after some discussion, was adopted by the committee. Mr. Stephens also pointed out the insufficiency of the playground acconimodation for the children in very cold weather, and the committee directed Mr. Mines to re- lax the regulation SA to the admission of the chilthen to the homes during play time, this arrangement meeting Mr. Stephens' views.—The CHAIRMAN, in moving the adoption of the minutes, said that Mr. Stephens expressed himself very pleased with the improvement, generally speaking, of the management of the schools. He (the chairman) thought that was very satisfactory. (Hear, hear.)—The minutes were passed. SCHOOL TEES •COMMITTEE. This committee reported that foes had been granted in 90 cases, 30 of which were new and 60 old cases.—Mr. Bram- uunsr, in moving the adoption of the minutes, said the in- crease in the applicants was only what they expected at this time of the year.. The increase, he was sorry to say, was chiefly due to the depression in the fustian cutting trade. He thought this showed that the general trade of the town was not much worse, but-nearly all the fustian cutters except apprentices were thrown out of work.—Mr. Bnowsr seconded the adoption of the minutes, which were agreed to.

LOCAL NEWS.

MR. J. T.. Bstrwruut is announced to address his sup- porters on Monday next at Halton, on Friday next at Weston, on the Friday following at Aston, and to be present at a Mass meeting of Liberals at the Theatre Royal Runcorn, on the 28th inst. NOETEWICH DIVISION ELECTION AnUallOirldENTS.—Tbe election in the North wich Division Will take place on Tues- day, December let. In Runcorn there will be two polling places—for the voters in Runcorn North at the Market Hall, and for the South at Mr. Cooper's Ballroom, Station-road, and Waterloo Bridge. In the Market Hall the acting sheriff has engaged four shops as polling booths. In the first electors numbered from 1 to 539 will vote; 2nd 531 to, 1,016; 3rd 1,017 to 1,621; 4th 1,622 to 2,173. The dis- tinguishing letter is J. At the Bailment there will be two polling booths, the distinguishing letter of which is K. In the first the voters numbered from 1 te 450 will vote, and in the second from 451 to 913. Most of the out electors will vote in this latter place, Runcorn South including Weston and Clifton. At Aston which includes Dutton and Sutton, the polling place will be the Board School, and at Halton, which includes Norton and Stockbain, it is at the Parochial Schools. Arrangements have been made for counting tbe votes at Northwich the same night, and it is expected that the result will be known shortly before midnight. ALMANACS at Lawless Brothers, 5, Market-place, now on view.—Advt. FOOTBaLL.—Runcorn v. Mr. T. B. Sutton's Manchester Team.—A very interesting match took place at Runcorn on Thursday afternoon, the game being exceedingly east and pleasant, and eventually ended in a draw—one goal, two tries, and two minor points each. Teams :—Manchester Team : A. Smith (Broughton), back; Jordan (Brough- ton), Valentine (Swinton), and Roberts (Bury), three-quar- ter backs ; Mills (Swinton), and Farrell (Widnes), half- backs ; Seddon (Swinton), Eagles (Salford), Ashton, Hodgson. Miller (Broughton Rangers), Anderton (Wigan), Hughes, Gandy (Widnes), Ashton, (Warrington); forwards. Runcorn : T. Woods, back • Johnson, Speakman, and Lunt, three-quarter backs; H. Hughes and Andrews, half. backs ; Wright, Hoffiand, Barnes, Outten Joule, Clarke, Broady, Cot, and Faulkner, forwards. Referee: Mr. T. R. Sutton (" Athletic News.") RUNCORN BOARD OF GUAEDIANs.—The usual fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday afternoon, Lient.-Colonel Ashton presiding. There were also present Mr. Weir (vice-chairman), the Revs. J. J. Bryant, J. U., N. Tanner, and J. Lockwood. and Messrs. J. nhoiwttiaekse, r.JF. i sher, Mclntyre.s..j. WIDNES C.E.T.S.—The juvenile members gave an enter- tainment on '1 intraday evening to a crowded audiences. The Vicar occupied the chair. An excellent programme was gone through. BETHESDA CONGREGATIONAL CHAPEL, RIINCORN.—On Sunday evening next the second of the series of " People's Services" will take place. The Rev. J. D. Thomas will preach on " Lessons for the coming election." FAILURE AT WIDNES.—At the Liverpool Bankruptcy Court on Monday the case of re Ellins and Ellins was heard. The debtors were brothers, carrying on business at Widnes, and since the last examination one of them, Francis H. Rhine, had died. The Registrar said he was sorry to hear of the death of the debtor. At the request of the official receiver the examination was closed. Runconn BLUE RIBBON ARMY.—Mrs. Ward, who for the past eight months has conducted the Blue Ribbon Army in Runcorn,has departed for Waterfoot, near Bacup. On Monday evening, about 100 persons assembled in the Co- operative Hall to bid her farewell, and she was presented by Mr. R. Evans, on behalf of the members and friends of the mission, with a purse of money, as a token of respect and esteem. The proceedings were presided over by Mr. T. Cooke, and Messrs. S. Coventry, J. Wathington, J. Kirkham W. Shaw, and W. Faulkner; and Miss Mitchell (Widnes) and Miss Womersley took part. RUNCORN BURIAL Boann.—The monthly meeting was held at the cemetery offices on Wednesday. Mr. Littler Presided, and there were present Messrs. James Handley, Jr., H. Colburn, W. Whittaker. W. 13. Rogerson. W. Mellor, E. Laison,R. Morrie, and W. F. Salkeld (secretary). The Finance Committee reported that the fees for the past month amounted to £33 178 101. The secretary's report stated that the interments for the seven months ending October 25 were 192; corresponding period last year, 218: decrease, 26. The fees received daring the same period amounted to £202 ss; last year,. £238 13s id; decrease, £36 ss. There was no other business of public interest. STRuGGLE WITH A LUNATIC AT WIDNES —On Tuesday, Mr. Scannell, relieving officer for Widnes, obtained an order for the committal to Rainhill Asylum of Edward Hughes, a chemical labourer, residing at 21, Pitt-street, Widnes. Hughes is a most powerful man, and when he was abont to be removed from his home he became very violent, fought, bellowed, and struggled like a wild beast, and it took the efforts of three policemen and the relieving officer to get him into the vehicle. He was in a complete state of frenzy, and he made such dangerous attacks upon those who had charge of him that eventually he had to be handcuffed. His removal caused great commotion in the neighbourhood. CHESHIRE AND Lattcasntan P B. 13. SOCIETY, Rues- co.--The annual meeting of this Society, better known as Holy Trinity Building Society, took place in Trinity School, on Thursday evening, under the presidency of Mr T. Sinister. There was a large attendance of mem- bers. In their report the committe state that the net profit of the society during the past year amounted to £1,366 183 sd, which would pay a dividend of £4 7s per cent. on the share capital, but owing to the number of withdrawal notices still remaining undiacharged, this dividend could not be paid. Mr T. Simister was re- elected president, and Mr. Alfred Buck was appointed a trustee in place of Mr. Peter Briscoe. A TRAMP'S Erna AT RUNCORN.—Mr. J. E. Wortley, the deputy coroner, held an inquest at the Sesseions House, Runcoin, on Monday, touching the death of a tramp, whose name is unknown. The man, who was about fifty years of age, 5 feet 5 inches in height, dark complexion, whiskers and hair turned grey. came to the town, on Thursday, and went to Phillips's lodging-h 01155, 35. Fryer•street. tie got his living by begging. He appeared to be very ill, and on Saturday night a fellow lodger heard him groaning loudly. Dr. McDougall was sent for, but the man's condition was hopeless, and he died shortly afterwards. Dr. McDougall deposed that there was nothing suspicious in the death. A verdict of natural causes was returned. ESCAPED LUNATICS AT RUNCORN.— Considerable excite- ment was caused at Top Locks, Runcorn, on Tuesday after- noon, by the strange actions of two men attired in " asylum clothing." It was soon bruited abroad that they were dangerous lunatics from Chester, and information was given to the police. P.S. Walley and Constables Egerton and Dale, after a long search, found the men secreted in a cellar in Gilbert-street, and they were placed in charge of a warder, who conveyed them back to Chester the same evening. The names of the men are Wm. Lamb, from Runcorn, and Win. Kirby, of Crewe, and they had escaped along with another lunatic from the asylum on the prerions night by jumping through a window. ANOTHRH SWING BOAT FATALITY —At Runcorn Sessions House, on Monday, Mr. J. E. Worslev. the deputy coroner, held an inquiry into the circumstances iaf the death of John Turner, 18 years of age, who was a labourer at Messrs. VVigg Brothers and Steele, and lived in Malcolm-street. On Saturday night Turner, whilst in a swing boat on the fair ground, lost his hat. When be alighted he endeavoured to reach his hat from beneath a boat which was in motion. He was struck on the head and rendered insensible. Dr. McDougall and Dr. Robinson examined the deceased, and found him suffering from a contused fracture of the skull and compression as well as paralysis. lie died on Sunday morning. A verdict of accidental death was returned. RUNCORN CHURCH MISSIONARY SOCIETY.—The annual missionary sermons were preached at Runcorn Parish Church in the morning and at Runcorn Holy Trinity Church in the evening. Toe Rev. A. R. Cavalier was the preacher. On Monday evening the usual meeting was held in Holy Trinity Schoolroom, Mr. F. A. Lake in the chair. The Rev. W. Preston reported that the Rnncorn Branch had remitted £57 las to the present society.—The Chairman thought they might cengratulate themselves on the amount. If we were, he said, to carry to the heathens the benefits of our commerce and civilization we must also supply them with the truths and benefits of the Gospel, because civiliza- tion alone nearly always brought with it increased tempta- tion and increased vices. The Rev. A. R. Cavalier gave an account of his labours in India. Votes of thanks concluded the proceedings. A GYMNAsiuM FOR RuloQ.—Arrangements have been made for opening the gymnasium which has been in process of formation for some time by the Runcorn The Drill Hall, Omagh the kindness of Captain Hazlehurst, J.P., has been placed at the disposal of the comal mittee. and the chief difficulty has the been reaerenrie. The building affords accommodation for several hundred performers. The gymnasium will be appropriately inaugu- rated on Thursday, the 19th. by a grand assault-at-arms, in the Public Hall, by members of the Liverpool Gymna- sium. Mr. Alexander will deliver a lecture On that °M- elon. This gentleman is taking the greatest Interest in the success of the undertaking. He bee been engaged by the committee te provide all the apparatus, and will in addi- tion, without fee or reward, attend at the Drill Hall one night each week to give instruction and conduct the varia ons exercises. The committee confidently anticipate receiv- ing public support for an institution calculated to be so great a benefit to the town. Full particulars in our an- nouncement column. NEWTOWN MISsioN Cutrncit, RONCORIT.—The annual Congregational tea party was held on Thursday. There was a very large attendance of parishioners and friends. The tables were presided over by Miss Barclay, Miss Edwards ; Mesdames Whittaker, Robert Goret, Marwood, Lightburn, Poison, and White. Subsequently an entertain- ment took place in the schoolroom, under the presidency of the Rev. R. Edwards, curate in charge, who delivered an appropriate address.—On the motion of the Rev. T. M. Amason, a vote of thanks was accorded to the lay readers, the choir, the organist, and the churchwardens.—Mr. Armson spoke in terms of high praise of Mr. C. Pownall, the organist and conductor.— Mr. G. Summerfield addressed the meeting, remarking with satisfaction upon the progress made by the mission during the past year. An interesting programme was gone through, the following taking part— Mists Horton, Messrs. C. Pownall, R. Morris, R. Moore, W. Howorth, J. Riley. and J Bowles. The choir gave several part songs in capital style. Great amusement was caused by a stump oration en " The Franchise Bill" delivered by Mr. A. E. Hawkins. RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.—A special meeting of this Board was held or Thursday morning. Mr. R. Shaw presided, and there were present—Messrs. P. Speakman, Taylor, White, Fisher, Lake, Lightburn, Imision, Whit- taker, Glace, Dobson, W. H. Linaker (law clerk), and E. Marshall (secretary).—Mr. Speakman said he bad given the usual notice that the vacancy caused by the death of Mr. Norman should be filled by Mr. W. J. Shores. Since the last meeting of the Board, however, Mr. Shores had intimated that he could not possibly attend to the duties at present, and wished his name to be withdrawn. As Mr. Wm. Mellor, of Church, received the highest number of votes of the can- didates who were not. successful at the last election, he moved that that gentleman be selected.—Mr. Lightburn seconded the motion and said if Mr. Shores had been pro- posed he should have moved an amendment in order to affirm the principle that the voice of the ratepayers should be heard.—Mr. Lake supported.—A short discussion took place against establishing a hard and fast rule that the un- successful candidate who received the highest number of votes at an election should be appointed to the first vacancy.—Mr. Mellor was elected unanimously. WIDNES CATHOLICS AND FREE EDUCATION —On Tuesday night an entertainment, at which about 2,000 persons were present., was given in St. Mary's Roman Catholic Schools, Widnes. During the interval, the Rev. James Clarke who presided, said Mr. Cbamberlain was agitating for free educa- tion, and there Was a school of advanced Radicals of which he was the very type. There was a lot of them in Paris, and when the people became aware of what they had done they certainly would not entrust their children to being taught in schools presided over by such men as Mr. Cham- berlain. (Cheers.) In the town of Widnes the Board school educated something like 200 scholars less than the denominational schools. The Catholics supported their own schools, and the Board schools were maintained out of the rates. Supposing education was made free, according to Mr. Chamberlain's plan, the people would be taxed double as much as they are now, and they would have to pay the tax as long as they were householders. (Hear, hear.) He believed Mr. Muspratt to be a good man, and that if he were an Emperor he would give the Catholics free educa- tion in the manner they desired, and in the form in which he spoke of it in his address ; but Mr. Chamberlain was too active for him. He believed Mr. Muspratt to be an ex- cellent man and sincere in what be said, but be was only a unit in the sum total, and like a buck,t of water in the Grand Canal at Dublin. (Cheers.)—The programme was then proceeded with. MERSEY MISSIOSS TO SELMER, BrewOttN.—The weekly meeting of the Mersey Missions Band of Hope took place on Vonday evening. Mr. W. Shaw presided, and therei was a large audience. A programme of songs, recitatitens, was gone through, Mr. G. Howard' acting as the accom- panist. POLICE Cr:llmm AT litneconn.—Sergeant Johnson, ef Frodsharn, Mee been promoted to the position of inspector at Runcorn, in place of Inspector Roche Sergeant Whalley, of Runcorn, is to be transferred tol Fredshace, and his posi- tion will be filled by P.C. Egerton, advanced to the rank of sergeant. P.C. Breeze is transferred to Weston. RUNCORN MILE DEALERS US TROUBLE.—At Runcorn Police Court on Monday, John Morris, milk dealer, Green- way-road, was charged with having in his possession two measures that were not of the standard required by the Board of Trade. ' Georae Purslow, James Ashbrook, John Smith, and Thomas Litchfield were charged with a like offence.—Superintendent Leah proved the case, and a fine of Is and costs was imposed in each instance RUNCORN STAR R-BOWEETT BUILDING SOCIETY.— An appropriation in connection with the first of the Runcorn Societies took place on Thursday night, in the Primitive Methodist Schoolroom, Frodshatn. Mr. P. Riley presided. In the first ballot No. 149 was drawn, but as the bolder was declared to be in arrest, a second ballot was taken, resulting in the number of Mr. George Savage, of Weston Point, being drawn, entitling the holder to £2OO for 121- years, free of interest. ST. JOHN'S PRESBYTERIAN SUNDAY SCHOOL, RUNCORN The anniversary services were held on eunday, and the Rev. Professor Edwards, of Bala, preached morning and evening to large congregations. In the afternoon the choir and children rendered the service of song entitled " Read- ings from Old Humphrey's Portfolio." The narrative was read by Mt. John Humphreys, and during an interval the Rev. Professor Edwards gave an address on" Music." The collections amounted to £9. A WIDNES WOMAN'S WISH GRATIFIED —At Widnes Po'ice Court on Monday Margaret Kenny, an elderly woman, was charged with doing wilful damage to a window.—P.C. Steele said on the previous day the prisoner came into the police station and asked to be locked up. He told tier he could not imprison her, as there was no charge preferred against her. She stated she would not go away, and that she would be locked up. Prisoner then left the office, and deliberately broke one of the windows.—She was committed to prison for 14 days. TERRIBLE DEATH OF A CHILD AT WIDNES.— On Wed- nesday afternoon, Mr. W. T. Husband, the deputy coroner, held an inquest at the Castle Hotel, Moss Bank, touching the death of Ralph Mousdell, infant son of Thomas Moos. deli, cooper, 10, Warrington-road. On Sunday the Ist inst. the child was in the cradle. On the floor close by was a pan containing boiling water. By some means the child fell from the cradle into the water head first. and received such injuries that it died on the following Sunday. Dr. McCambridge was the medical attendant. A verdict of accidental death was returned and there was no euspicion of neglect against the parents. ACCIDENTS AT WlONES.—Whilst engaged repairing a vitriol chamber at the works of Messrs. Hall and Shaw, on Monday, Joseph Houghton slipped and fell a distance of 20 feet from the ladder on which he was standing. He sus- tained a serious shock to the system, accompanied by lice raorrhage, and was taken to the hospital where he.was at- tended by Dr. McDonnell. The injured man's home is at 75, Beamont-street.—The engineer of the "Calder" steam ship was stepping from the vessel to the quay side at West Bank when he slipped between the boat and the dock. He Was, however, quickly rescued without ill results. POACHING NEAR RUNCORN.—Jobn Foster was summoned to Runcorn Police Court on Monday charged with trespass- ing on the land of Mr. Chadwick Clifton, in search of game.—Mr. Dreaper defended.—Mr. Howe, gamekeeper on the Aston Estate, deposed that there was gems on the field where the defendant was treepeesing.—P.C. Egerton said he saw the defendant fire a gun on the field. He afterwaids took the gun off the defendant, who said he was very sorry for what he had done, but he had only been shooting "pee- wits."—Mr. Dreaper stated his client was going along the footpath in the field for the purpose of shooting along the side of the river Weaver. He called a witness, who stated there was no garoe in the field.—A fine of 108 and costs, us 6d, was imposed. FELONIES AT WlPNee.—At Widnes Petty Sessions on Wednesday, Catherine Caffertv, a married woman with a young child in her arms, was charged with stealing a dress worth 'ls, the property of A. L. Collinge. pawnbroker, 9, Mersey-road, Widnes. On the morning of the sth inst. the prisoner was in the shop. On her departure the dress was missed, and she afterwards offered it in pledve at Mr. Imison's shop in Waterlon-road.— As this was the woman's first appearance, she was only fined 103, or 14 days.-- Patrick Moyer, a disreputable-looking fellow, was charged with stealing a pair of boots worth 10e, the property of Annie Jamison, pawnbroker, Annie-street. The hoots had disappeared in a similar manner to the dress in the last case, and the prisoner had attempted to pledge them.—He was sentenced to a month's imprieonment. SERIOUS ACCIDENT AT RUNCORN —Yesterday, Albert Watson, 20 years of age, who lives with his parents at Heath-road. Runcorn, met with a serious accident ou the railway. 'He was walking In the "four foot" of the line that runs from Weston Point Dock to Runcorn, and 'companion named 11,4wlinson was walking in the "six foot." When they arrived at the curve shoot three I quarter of a mile from the dock, an engine and I several waggons suddenly came upon them, and before Watson could step met of the way, he was knocked down The wheels of the engine passed over his right foot, which was smashed in a terrible fashion. He was brought to the railway station in a brake, and seen by Dr. MecDougell, who ordered his immediate removal to Liverpool Infirmary. In that institution it was foand necessary to amputate the foot just abeve the ankle. SHOPKEEPERS IN TROUBLE AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Police Coert on Wednesday, Thomas Kerr was summoned ' for keeping a refreshment bowie in Ann-street without a licence. Mr. Heal, supervisor. prosecuted, and the case was proved by Mr. Speechley. A fine of 5s and costs (143) was Imposed.—For selling half aa ounce of tobacco without a licence at her shop in Ann-otreet, Mrs. Ann Cannon was Sued 103 and costs —Mr. Richard Webster, grocer, Albert- Toed, wee fined 20s and ooste !Or Wring in his poseesidoa a pair of cannier scales witich were halt an Mina out of balance. Mr. Webster said the scales were probably Injured by an accident that took place a short time pre- vionaly.—For having a pair of scales which were a quarter Of an ounce out of balance, Mr. Frank Lawrinson, grocer ana provision dealer, Albert-road, was fined lOs and costs. Mr. Peters, solicitor, defended. ATTEMPTED OUTRAGE UPON A GIRL AT bIINCKNIN.,-". before Mr. James Handley, at Runcorn Police Court, oa Tuesday, Moss Williams,3s years of age, a native of Mold, who had been working in Runcorn, was charged with hav- ing, on the 31st October, attempted to commit a rope upon Martha Ann Boatock, 12 years of age, who lived with her parents at 60, Ashbridge.street. On the night of the date mentioned the prisoner took the girl upon the fair ground and " treated " her into the swing boats, and with sweeta, dm. About eleven o'clock he took th.l girl into a lonely part near Castle Rock, and he attempted to criminally as- sault her. Three men appemed noon the scene, and gave the prisoner a rather rough handling, and be absconded. On Monday last, P.S. Neild received the prisoner into cus- tody at Oldham, where his sister keeps a beerhouse. He was committed to the Chester Assizes for trial. VIOLENT STRUGGLE WITH A PRISONER AT WIDNES.— Martin Murray, whose heed was enveloped in surgical ban- dages, was charged at Widnes Police Court on Monday with being drunk and disorderly on the 7th inst. and as- saulting P C. Pitt.—Complainant stated that at five minutes to eleven he found the defendant at Moss Bank in a drunken and disorderly condition. He was shouting and wanting to fight with two men who were in the road, and who made a complaint to witness that the prisoner had followed them from Widnes. Witness asked the prisoner to go away, and he did en; but he eventually found prisonar a few minutes after in Moss Bank wanting to fight. - Witness told him he would see him home, whereupon prisoner struck him twice in the face. Witness then got the prisoner to Mr. Griffin's door, where a struggle ensued, and witness was knocked down on the stone steps by the prisoner. While Murray was being put out of the hones—for Mr. Griffin refused to allow him to come in—witness fell on his back on the stone step, and his back was injured. Prisoner then attempted to strangle witness, and was so violent that the constable had to hit him on the head with his staff About half an RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY. hoar afterwards P.C. ROBBERIES AT WIDNES. George Swindles wan charged at Widnes Police Court, on Monday, with stealing into pigeons, the property of:Edward Weir. Mr. Knowles defended. Weir lives at 33, Travis- street, and the prisoner had lodzed at the house for the past eight months. On the 31.0 t October the priaoner went borne drunk, and Mrs. Weir requested him to leave. Next morn- ing she saw that the pixtron cote had been broken into, and four pigeons taken. The prisoner admitted having taken the b ids and sold them to various persons. Mr. Knowles contended that the birds belonged to the prisoner, who was, however, fined 20s, or seven days. The money wan paid.— John Shannon was charged with stealing a pocket handker- chief, the property of Luke Whitney, a labourer living in Major Cross-street. Between nate and ten on the previous night Whitmey went into the Royal Hotel. Hutchinson- street, where the prisoner abstracted his handkerchief from his pocket. Whitney thought the man wan playing a tricl:, but when he requested a return of the article the prisoner struck him a violent blow on the nose. The prisoner, who admitted his guilt to P.C. Laing, was tined los, or 14 days. —Thomas Stanley, 15 years of age, a youth without home who goes about the river in flat', was charged with stealing a jacket, a basket, and a cop and saucer, worth 22*. the pro- perty of the Manchester. Sheffield. and Lincolnshire Rail- way Co„ On the 24th September Walter Rowevbreakernam of 4. Carlyle-terrace, saw the articles safe in bin van on the marsh. On Saturday, the 7th inst., he saw the prisoner wearing the coat, and bed him taken into custody. The prisoner pleaded guilty, and was senteneted to seven days' hard labour.

VOLUNTEER CONTEST AT ST, HELENS, The annual ride match closing the season took place on Saturday, at Sutton Range, between representative teams of I the St. Helens and Preacot companies, and the Sutton and Widnes companies. The st. Helens. and Presoot team dth 912 lbed, an aceoraing to arrange- ment betwcen the two captains (Major White and Sergeant West) all present were to ahoot, the lowest scores to be ! knocked off to reduce the number to 29 on each aide. The I ondittons were Wimbledon targets and ecorlng ; distances , -200 and 500 yards; seven shots at each. The weather I was faveurable, although the light was not very good.l Scores ReenS and Prescot Companies: Sergeant aim 65 points sergeant West 847 Sergeant P. Byrne 82,1 Private R. McGill 01. Sergeant Waxen Private J. Bag- t ley 60, Lieutenant J. L. Wolfenden 56, Private R. Preston 58, ?rivets J. Cannington 55, Private J. Hewitt 55, Private R. Norbury 54. Private R. Edwards 53. Edwards 48, Sergeant- Instructor PO. litt 47, Private Fothera 47, total 1 095 points.- Sutton and Widnes Companies; Private Foster 65 pointa, Bugler White 62, Private N. P. Neill 60, Major White 59, Corporal Clare 57, Private Campbell 57, Corporal Taylor 57, Private P. Webster 56, Sergeant Bate 55, Private W. F. Newton 52, Colour-Sergeant McKennon 51, Sergeant P. Lucas 48, Sergeant-Instructor IL Winfield 45, Sergeant Dwerryheuse 41, Sergeant-instructor Hills 33, total 1,045 points. The St. Helens and Prescot Companies thus won by 50 points. After the match the teams sat down to an excellent tea at the Fleece Hotel. Major White presided, and he was supported by Major Wilcocks, Lieutenant Wol- fenden, and Sergeant-Major Tyson. Sergeant West gave an interesting account of the shooting during the past year. Na less a sum that £360 in money, challenge cups value £135, and eight badges had been won from home during the season. Major White also referred with pleasure to the presence amongst them that day of so many young shots, and trusted they would endeavour next season to makt themselves thoroughly efficient in the use of the rifle, no that, as the older shots retired from active work, they might be able to take their places, and maintain in the future the high reputation attained in the past and present by the 21st L.R.V. (Applause.)

FooTBALL. --The Football Times for Wednesday last contains a portrait of Mr. J. E. Warren, the popu- lar captain of the Warrington Football Club. We shall endeavour to find room in our next issue for the sketch which is given of Mr. Warren's career at an athlete.—Sankey a. Moss Bank White Star, Widnes: These teams met for the first time this season on the ground of the latter on Saturday. The vicitors managed to secure a victory by two tries and three minor points to one try and one minor point. LIBERAL AND CONSERVATIVE INDIAN FINANCE. —A COMPARISON.—Mr. I. S. Leadam, gives a com- parison between the actual cost of the Indian mili- tary expenditure under Lord Lytton (Conservative) and his predecessor, Lord Northbrook (Liberal,) The figures are taken from the official statement, and include "Operations in Afghanistan," and are as follow 187-2 (Gard Northbroak's firs A year) £l4 734,083 1872 3 1873 4 1871-6 1075 6 (Lord Lytton's first year) 14,242,848 1876-7 1877.8 1878-0 1879-40 21.632.880 18804 (regular estimate) These figures byno means tell the whole tale. Not- withstanding this increase in the burdens upon the natives, the account of the Afghan war was by no means settled. When Lord Lytton left India by far the greater part of the cost remained unpaid. The land cess and the license tax, imposed by Loid Lytton, were appropriated for war purposes to the amount of £670,000. Of fifteen and a half millions, cost of Afghan war, the English taxpayer has had to pay five millions. The estimate of the cost for 1880-1 was £1,060,000 ; the actual cost was £10,364,497—a difference of .£6,304,497 ! WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held At Altorde Chambers on Tuesday. Mr. F. Goasage presidedond there were pre- sent Dr. O'Keeffe. S. Sadler, F. H. Pankhurst, T. Hand- ley, E. Carey, D Wri4ht. B. Dutton, F. Heve, Jno. Taylor, H. Gaskell,. junior, D. Foreter, J. T. Allen (clerk).

div.head: LOCAL BOARDS AND THE .BALLOT.
div.p: LOCAL BOARDS AND THE .BALLOT.

The Chairman said there was a long letter from the Swin- ton Local Board, asking other public bodies to petition that election by ballot should he adopted by the various local boards throughout the country. He added that they were about to have an entirely new style of Parliament, and one of its first duties would be the reconsideration of local Government, and in that of course would come the election and government by local boards, and a variety of other things in the shops of county councils, lie therefore thought the letter might lie on the table until some future time.—The letter was ordered to lie on the table.

RAILWAY RATES. The Clerk read a circular letter from the Lancashire and :Cheshire Conference of Local Authorities on railway rates and terminal charges, and suggesting that the candidates for Parliament should be asked if they would support leyisla- tion in favour of relieving these heavy burdens imposed on trade by the railway comoanies.—The Chairman thought this was a matter in which the Board could not take any action ; it was a eubject for individual action.—lt was de- cided that the letter he on tile table.
THE GENERAL ELECTION.

... The Clerk said the sheriff had made application for the use of the Board•room in which to count the votes at the Parliamentary election, and he promised that he oould have the room subject to the Approval of the Board. He did not see any objection to the arrangement himaelf. In reply to the Chairman, he said the election would be held on the 2nd December.—Mr. Wright moved, and Mr. Taylor ercooded, that the room could be used for the purpose named free of charge.—Carried without dissent.

div.head: NUISANCES.
div.p: NUISANCES.

WM. Halliday, of 2, Pitt-street, wrote complaining of a nuisance caused by the accumulation of water in the cellar of his konse and in the yard; be stated it caused a great lees at revenue to him, and although he had complained fre- qnently to Inspector Dickson he had received no redress. C. Cliffe, of 56 and 58, Waterloo-road, complained that owing to the bad sewetage his premises were partially flooded, and that he had been compelled to remove his horse to other premises.—At a later stage of the meeting, Dr. O'Keefe explained that works were in progress at present which would prevent a recurrence of the nuisances com- plained of. On Monday last he visited the premises in icompany with the inspector, and there was then really very little to complain of.

GAS AND WATER COMMITTEE. The minutes of the Gas and Water Committee stated that the S. and M. Railway Company had connected water to offices without the Board's sanction, and the committee re- commended that legal proceedings be taken against, the company unless a satisfactory explanation be given.—The minutes were adopted on the motion of Mr Gaskell,seconded by Mr. Taylor.

HIGHWAT MATTERS. The Righway Committee recommended that the tender of Mr. D. Hirst for excavations at Crow Wood £99, and at the promenade £25, be accepted. In reply to a letter from Mr. I J. Midwood, the Clerk was instructed to say that plans were in preparation for making Wellington and Marsh streets.— The minutes were confirmed on the motion of Mr. Carey, seoonded by Mr. Du, ton. 1 INCREASED USEFCIMESS OF THE ACCIDENT HOSPITAL. GRATIFYING HEALTH REPORT. The Medical Officer had reported to the Health Corn. mittee that during October there were 84 births and 21 deaths, being at the rate respectively of 37.33 and 937 per 1,000. Four of the deaths occurred among children under one year and four amongst children between one and five years ; one death resulted from zymotic disease. The nuisance inspector reported that two children. bad been attacked with scarlet fever, but both were recovering. Letters had been received from Drs. Booth, McLennan, Mc- Cambridge, McDoonell. and O'Neil, respecting the coin- enittee's proposals with regard to the notification of infec- : Omni disease. These gentlemen promised to help the corn- ; mittee, but the majority refused to report all cases.—The committoo decided to give notice to rescind the resolution l passed at the last meeting, on this subject, viz: to pay a fee of 2a 6d for each erase of infections disease reported,— Dr. O'Keeffe, in moving the confittnetiou Of the minutes, referred to the uhlett notifiCation of disease. The gebtlerbea in the town refused to report all cases, ' Considering that many of their best patients might not like it. They were willing, however, to give every assistance in; their power to the Board and the sanitary inspector in onier to prevent the spread of zymotic disease. Under these circumstances the committee thought it advisablu to rescind the resolution passed at the last meeting. Referring to the nulsenee from the Rainhill sewage farm, ! Dr. O'Keeffe said that Dr. Frankland had analysed the samples of water taken in the presence of the Urban Authority and the Rural Sanitary Authority, and the re- . salt was very far from satisfactory. The water contained AR immense amount of poisonous matter, and it was thought , advisable to instruct the clerk to again call the attention of ;the Local Government Board to the subject, and it was ! I hoped that they would cause the Rural Sanitary Authority . to abate the nuisance they were inflicting upon the tawnsbio of Widoea.—Mr. l'aukhurat seconded the motion.—Mr. Hue- hand ohjeCted to the rescinding of the motion with regard to the notification of infectious diseases; half a loaf was j better than no bread, rod the medioal men were willing to notify some cases; Om resolution had batter stand.— Mr. Carey agreed with Mr. Husband. He understood, however, from Dr. O'Keeffe, that the Board would getl-eports of the majority of cases without any fee at all, and if the members could be assured of that he would be I quite satisfied. He would rather not pav any fee.— Dr. GKeeffe then called attention to the eminently satisfac- tory state of the health of the township at present. The death rate was only nine per thousand and he did not think there was a town in England where the death rate was so ; low-. In the United Kingdom for the past ten months the , death rare was 16 per 1000 from all causes, and 247 from zy- motic causes; in St. Helens, from all causes. 17 8, zymotic 36; in \Vivo, all causes 18.8, zymotic 618 ; Southport, all causes 178, zyenotic 3 74; Warrington, all causes 16.1, zvrootic 220; in Widnes all causes 167, zymotic I.—The minutes were then posited.

_....___ . FINANCE. The Finance Committee had received letters from Messrs. Lancashire and Earesh.w offecing to accept an in- creased rent of £7 lOs per annum for the Board's offices, Alforde Chamber, f rem the 29th September last. It was recommended that the offer be accepted subject to six months' notice.—Accounts amounting to £2,797 Ils Id were passed for paymene—The minutes were approved on the motion of Mr. T. Hendley. THE APPOINTMENT OF CLERK OF WORKS. The minutes of the General Purposes Committee cone 1 tamed the following paragraph with regard to the appoint- ' ment of clerk of works to the public offices:—" Letter, 26th October, from W. Hodgkinson submitted. The members of the committee, with all deference to the decision of the Board, desire respectfully to protest against the method ad- ooted in making the recent appointment, and to record their opinion, that in all cases choice of public servants should be ' made solely with regard to personal merit and fitness, and without reference to local or other considerations."—Mr. Carey moved the adoption of the minutes. TRE "GRATE RUNCORN rorr."—James Erinshaw, who declares himself " The Grate Runcorn Poet," brought an action to recover from James Woods, of Milt Brow band- master, the sum of £l, money alleged to ie due upon an agreement made between the plaintiff and defendant.— Erinshaw stated that he was engaged to sing at the grand military concert held recently. The defendant denied having made such an agreement, and his Honour said he could not think that an engagement had been made with any amount lof seriousness between the parties. He gave judgment for the defendant with costs.

TIM BANKRUPTCY Acr.—William Lightfoot, whose wife appeared, was ordered to pay £7 due under an .ider under the Bankropccy Act, and his Honour threatened that if he failed that next court day he would d scharge the order altogether, and leave the defendant to the mercy of his crcditors. Mr. Lake appeared on behalf of the acting Credi- tor, Mr. H. Wkite.

i the Board meeting at all. The protest of the committee r seemed to him absurd, and he lodged his protest against its I protest, which in his opinion did not amount to much. At (the same time, if the committee were annoyed, he would move that they pass a resolution of condolence with the General Purposes Committee for having its resolution over- hauled.—The Chairman : I don't think that is before the Board.—Mr. Husband: I should be glad to :zing it forward if the General Purposes Committee feel it keenly.—Mr. Wright moved that the paragraph be expunged from the minutes—Mr. Husband seconded the amendment,which was supported by Mr. Sadler and Dr. O'Keeffe.-Mr. Carey again having enunciated his views that a man should be appointed to a position in consequence of his abilities and fitness for the post, and rot for merely local considerations, the amendment was put to the meeting and carried by nine votes to three.—Messrs. Gaskell, Handley, and Carey were the minority.

PROPOSED TOWN NALL. Dr. O'Keeffe then moved the motion of which he had given notice, that the entire plans of the public offices and town hall be carried out forthwith.—The Chairman took exception to the words 'town hall:" saying that their use was confined to boroughs.—Dr. O'Keeffe : I expect Widnes will be a borough soon.—The Chairman : God defend us ; I hope not !—Dr. O'Keeffe proceeded to say that there were no places of interest in Widnes which the residents could visit except those fine structures they saw about them where the worship of Bacchus was carried on, he did not know whether with benefit and advantage to the minds of the worshippers. It was a pity there was no place except the Science and Art School, for which they had to thank ome of the generous donors of Widnes, where the people could go for intellectual pleasure and advanceme .t, and that was only on a Saturday night. Then there was no place except the Volunteer Hall where meetings and balls could be held, and the proprietor of that building charged from £2 lOs to ZS per night. He contended that the revenue from the town hall if erected would be at least £lO per week, and would pay the interest upon the £lO,OOO that would have to be expended. The public offices were expec. ted to cost about. £6,000 and the town hall aboat £lO,OOO, and for this sum there would be a place for the fire engine and a fire hell—and what use was a fire engine without a fire bell ? The Market Hall itself might be burned some night without anybody knowing it. There would also be accommodation for a free library and a free newsroom, and the people of the town would have a atrnc- tore of which they would be proud. He had not the slightest doubt that some of their millionares—merchant princes as they were called in Venice long ago—would have the generosity of Mr. Brunner, of Northwich, and present them with a number of books. If the entire structure was not proceeded with, when the Town Hall had to be erected, a certain portion of the public offices would have to be pul- led down at a cost of £l,OOO. and if they proceeded with the work now, that amount would be saved. He was quot- ing the words of the architect —Mr. Forster seconded the motion—Mr. Husband said it appeared to him that Dr. O'Keeffe had been having a sort of day dream, had been building castles in the air, and bad been dreaming abeut legacies from this person and the other person. He did not see the necessity for building the Town Hall at present, when they decided not to erect the hospital in its ee- tirety so tbat they would not burden the rates. Let them build necessities before they built luxu- ries. There was just the possibility of the rates being increased by free education—(cries of "no, no,")— and oonsidering the great outcry at present about high rates, he did not see the force of going into this expense unless it was a necessity that the Town Hall should be erected. He moved an amendment that consideration of the subject be postponed for six menthe.—Mr. Dutton : Oh, for ever! —Mr. Husband : Sine die.—Mr. Dutton seconded the mntion.—Mr. Carey said a town hall would add very much to the culture of the town in many ways, but his own im- pression was that they could not afford to erect one at pre- sent. —The Clerk said be had calculated that the annual cost would be £578. requiring a rate of lid it the X.—Mr. Carey : We should want £lO per week to addition to the cost of lighting and heating. He was afraid they could not make it pay.—Dr. O'Keeffe thought they would get a rev- enue of £lO per week.—Mr. Carey suggested that the clerk should obtain information of the revenue derived from town halls in other places.—Mr. Husband withdrew his amend- ment in favour of this suggestion, which Dr. 0 Keeffe also agreed to act upon. The meeting then concluded.

THE TEMPERANCE PARTY IN THE NORTHWICH DIVISION. On Wednesday evening an adjourned meeting of tem- perance delegates, representing the various temperance orgaoisations in Runcorn, took place is the lecture-ball of Betheeda Chapel. Mr. Charles Littler took the chair, and called upon Mr. J. D. Jones to read the following I report of the deputation which waited upon the two Can- I didates for Northwich on the question of Local Option :—" The deputation, consisting of Messrs. John Wilson, Thomas Htesom, Daniel Biebrown, Thomas Cooke and J. D. Jones, waited upon Mr. Brunner in accordance with the resolution of the meeting held on the 24th June, and laid the Local Option resolution before him. In re- sponse to the irquiries of the deputation, Mr. Brunner agreed to support the resolution, end expressed himself as decidedly is favour of the question of licensing being settled ,by the ratepayers. On the question of the Sunday closing of public-houses in England, Mr. Brunner said be was unprepared to support an imperial measure for the I whole of the country, preferring to leave the question in the hands of the people. He would not, however, oppose such a Bill, and would hea,tily support a Sunday Ciosing Bill for Cheshire. The deputation waited noon Mr. Verdin I also, and after submitting die same resolution for eis con- sideration. he said in reply th it be preferred. l.p.fine• xp-es- ; sing a definite opinion, to wait until the reallution WRS , embodied in a measure and brought before the House of ; Commons the mean time he would give the nroposal his 1 best consideration. He fee-owed the Sunday Clasing Bill. I but would not pledge himself to support it. Mr. Verdin reminded the deputation that he had been a total Abstainer till hit life, and thought that such a fact ought to he con- sidered by the teetotallers in the division as a sufficient , guarantee that his sympathies were with them in , the objects they sought to attain, without their endeavour- ing to extract a pledge from him to support any definite measure." • On theenotion of Mr. William Heathington, seconded by Mr. James Bisbrown, a resolution to support Mr. Brunneri the Liberal candidate, us passed unaninspinly

_ COLLISION ON TNII Rivast.--Messrs. Thompson, McKay, and Co., carriers, Manchester, sued Mr. Richard Abel, boat owner, Runcorn, for £1 ls 8d for damage alleged to have been cicne to the boat Gerty. On the 3rd April the Getty was being pulled into the tidal dock at Raneorn by several men, when the flat "Mersey," belonging to the defendant, just released from a tug, collided .wit b It, and stove in several planks. Captain Garnett stated be shouted to the man in charge of the Mersey to starboard his helm, but he put it aport. There was no defence to the action, and the defendant was ordered to pay the amonnt with costs in 14 days. A FATHER'S DEBTS.—Williatn Blythe, clothier, High. street, Runcorn, sued John Gittens, of Egerton, as executor de son tort of William Gittens, deceased, for £22 for goods supplied. William Gittens was drowned come months ago, and the defendant had appropriated £2O club money, in order to pay himself for money lent to the deceased. His Honour held that the defendant must first of all pa), the decetteefl's first debts and he gave a verdict for the Man or A BOAT.—William, Richard, and Joseph Weed- all sued Joseph Taylor, Waterman, Brook-street, for £9 3s tlid far the hire of a boat.—Mr. Yearslev appeared for the plaintiff, who obtained a verdict of £7 Ba, to be paid at the rate of 16s per month.

florin Tnittattra.—Frederick Savage, of Pickow Farm, was sued by Sarah Bancroft, shopkeeper, for El ss, damage alleged to have been done by the defendant's horse. Mr. Dreaper defended. The horse was in charge of a trainer, walking along Church-street, when it backed into the plain- tiff's window, and smashed it, besides damaging the sweets. —His Honour held that the defendant was not liable, and that the trainer would not be liable unless negligence Was proved.—Mr.Dreaper. said his client had offered the plain- tiff ltits on the previous night without prejudice, and as the plaintiff had had to repair the window, he did not wish to press for costs.—His Honour nonsuited the plaintiff With.. out costs._

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. MoNPAT.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), Aid. Chandley. Councillor Greening, Alderman Holmes, and Mr. John Fairclough. MISCELLANEOUS. •—• The following were dealt with for drunkenness :—Thomas Cummings, in Bridge-street, on Saturday evening, fined 5s including costs; Mary Smith, in Sankey-street, discharged on promising to leave the town ; William Kay' at the Police Station on Friday.discharged on promising to leave the town; Thornas Flannery, in Butter- market-street, on Saturday night, and also for committing an assault upon P.C. Neill, sent to prison for a month; Michael Cal lighan and Bodelia Knockton, sent to prison for a month; Michael Griffin and Michael Kilkane, fined ss, including costs, each.—Joseph Blakemore, for being drunk whilst in charge of a horse and trap in Horsemarket-street, was fined 5s and costs —James Gallagher, for committing a breach of the peace by fighting in Sharp-street, on the 16th August, boned over to keep the peace. Tazwr BY A GlRL.—Hannah Taylor (18), whose parents live at Latchford, was charged with stealing a pair of boots and other articles, the whole of the value of £1 17s 2d, the property of Mary Rimtner, domestic servant at the Golden Grove Inn. She was sent to prison for three months, with hard labour. TBIIESDAY.—Before Major Litton. DRUNIENNESS.—Mirgaret Preseall was sent to prison for seven days, and Elizabeth Glover for 14 days, for this offence. FBlDAY.—Before Captain Reynolds, Dr. Gornall, and Mr. John White.

MISCELIANECUS. Charlotte Plunkett, summoned by Alice Kenna for using threats, was difiraiSSed.--Brldget Rodan, an elderly woman, charged Kate Mcllermot with assaulting her on the 7th inst. The case was dismissed,

RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Before Mr. A. Thomas and Mr. James Handley. MISCELLANEOUS.—For being drunk on licensed premises and tieing obscene language, David Goben was fined 203 and costs.—A fins of 5s and costs was imposed upon James Sed• don for using obscene laugusge.—Jase Clare was fined fis and cop for being drunk and disorderly.

_DESPERATE AFFRAY AT ASHTON. A rOACHBIt 91107 : 4 (14MEEEJ3ER AFTREHENDRP, On Monday', at the Wigan County POliCO Court, Johd Green, a collier residing at 53, Scholes, Wigan, applied for a warrant against Marmaduke Webster, gamekeeper, Ash- ton, for doing him grievous bodily harm by shooting him in the face with a gun on the 22nd of October last.—A warrant was granted.—At the Police Court, on Tuesday, Marmaduke Webster was brought up, charged with shoot- ing Green. Mr. Lees appeared for the prisoner.—John Oreen, the prosecutor, said that about two o'clock on the morning of Thursday, the 22nd of October, he and five of his companions were in Garswood Park, belonging to Lord Gerard. He knew his companiane by eight, but he did not know their names. They bad six nets down. About two 'O'clock he saw three gamekeepers and two dogs, cud he ran towards his companions and said, " Now, lads, they are here." The gamekeepers ran after him, and one of them shouted to the others to "Come on," and stick together. When about 25 yards from witnese,the gamekeepers started throwing stones, and he and his companions retaliated in the same way. Then the keepers began to shoot at him and his mates, and they also blew their whistles. Two of the gamekeepers shot, and six or seven shots were fired altogether. The first shot that was fired struck witness in the face, and he fell to the ground crying out that he was shot. He got up again and the same gamekeeper fired once more, and the shot struck witness on the breast. One of the witness's companions then said, "Came on," and they took him away, and while he was being taken away he WAS again shot at, and the shot struck him in the leg. He could not saw, however, who fired the last shot as he had his back turned to the keeper. Tom Duke (meaning the prisoner) was the person who shot him in the face and breast. Witness's companions took him down the brow ond over the brook of water, and the keepers kept shooting at them as they went. His companions left him at Poolsteck. When he got home he was washed, and than he vomited nearly a pint of blood. He gave information to the police and went into the Infirmary on the 22nd of October, and came olt of the institution on the 6th inat By Mr. Lees: They had each a thick stick which would give a fellow a good whacking if he were hit with one. There were only six of them there. He had not seen the men since, and only sae/ them once before the night on which the affray took place. Witness had a good knife with him. His companions did not cry "Rip them up," neither did they shoat, "Bring pikele, and we will kill them all." They did not want to lose their nets, and they con- tinued stoning the keepers to keep them away. He and his friends had no guns with them. They picked the stones up on the road, and put them in the pockets before they went. They got some more in the park. He had never been up for poaching before. He had been several times for being eirunk and fighting, and he had also been up for burglary once and got nine months. Be got six months for break- ing into an office in 1878, and be had served several months for other offences. He did not know where his companions lived in St. Helens. By Superintendent Heywood WitneEs was quite certain that none of his par. ty treed firearms they stoned the keepers. -- P.C. Granthadt of Ashton, said he and P.S. Devlin were on duty On Garewood-road and heard reports of firearms coming from the direction of Lord Gerard's park, and they went to park entrance and were admitted. They saw the prisoner and ten keepers, who said there had. been poachers in the park, and that they had gone out over the wall. The keepers fild not appear to have been burt.—P.S. Devlin stationed at Haydock, gave corroborative evidence. He added that he apprehended the prisoner on Monday, the 9th inst., at Ash- ' ton Cross. Webster made no reply to the charge.—Dr. Buchanan, eenior house surgeon at the Wigan Infirmary, said the injured man came into the Infirmary about 7-30 on the 22nd October. lie examined him, and found 25 pellet marks over his chest, shoulders, and face, and there were two on the calf of the right leg. There were some bruises over his right shoulder, and his right eve, his only one, WAS bloodshot, and he could not see properly. As a result of the blow on the eve a cataract was forming, and there was an appearance of degeneration of the optic nerve, which was a still more serious matter, and there was a strong pool- bilitv that the man would become blind.—Mr. Lees said that as the assizes were SO near, he would not call any wit- nesses, but would advise the prisoner to reserve his defence. The prisoner was then committed to take his trial at the mains, bail being allowed. £100,000,000 in the COURT OF CHANCERY!—Cox é Co., 41, Boutbampton•bulldings. Holborn, London, W.C., leave just published a list of the heirs to this wealth. Reader, send a postal order for Is lid, and they will forward you this valu- able list, and if you find by it that you are entitled to any money or property claim your own. Cox A Co. will show you the way.—„Adrt. Miss Lavinia Heysett, of Teignmonth, who is at present living as barmaid at the Imperial Hotel, Plymouth., has lately been left a fortune of £70,000 by her uncle, William Howe Bolstancy. Robert Dixon Hewetson, described as a stockbroker, of Liverpool, was sentenced at the Nottingham Assiaes on Wednecday to 12 months' imprisonment for fraud in con- nection with a "syndicate." IRISH LAND ACT.—The first transaction under the Irish Land Purchase Act, the purchase by the tenants of their holdings On a property in Tyrone, has just been completed. The landlord will receive about 18 years' purchase, and the tenants will have less to pay than in their former circuits. stances. RIOT AT LIHRRICIL—A deplorable ill-feeling exists be- tween some et the townspeople and the military at Limer- ick, and on Tuesday night a serious riot arose out of it. A considerable number of the King's Royal' Rifles managed to smuggle their side arms out of barracks and made an attack on their adversaries. They appear tot have got the worst of the encounter, four or five of them being disabled, one having a leg broken. Fears are entertained of a renewal of the disturbance. LORD HARTINGTON AND LORD R. CHMICHILL.—The Marquis of Hartington, addressing the electors of the Itos- sendale division on Thursday evening. explained at some length his conduct with regard to the subjects on which he bad been attacked by Lord Randolph Churchill, and having justified himself on those matters, pointed out that his lord- ship in accusing him of want of principle had utterly failed to notice the consistent and ungrudging support that he bad given to the vast majority of Liberal measures during the past quarter of a century. With much force and sarcasm Lord Hartington retaliated upon Lord Randolph Churchill by examining the latter'e definition of the principles of the Tory Democracy, and said that a party with each a pro- gramme was deserving more of pity than of hatred.
