div.head: TRE EXA,MINER. SATURDA.Y, NOVEMBER 14, 1885
div.p: TRE EXA,MINER. SATURDA.Y, NOVEMBER 14, 1885

LIBERAL MEETING AT WARRINGTON. A largely-attended Liberal meeting was held in the Working-men's Mission School-room, Bank Quay, on Monday evening. The chair was taken by Mr. F. Monks, who was supported by Mr. McMinnies, M.P., Mr. W. Crosfield, J.P., Aid. John Crosfield, J.P., Mr. C. Broadbent, J.P., Mr. J. S. Green, Mr. H. Roberts, and Mr. A. Browne. Tbe CHAIRMAN, who was received with applause, said that at a recent Tory meeting Alderman Davies said that for the last five years, under a Liberal government, the trade and commerce of this country had been making a downward course. That was a definite statement and he for one had been looking to see how far that statement could be borne out by facts. There were methods by which they could ascertain whether it was true or not, and in his opinion the imports and exports of the country, the savings of the work- people, that was to say the money accumulated in the savings banks, and the income tax returns afforded the means of forming a very fair estimate as to whether the country was going forwards or backwards. What did they actually find? The Tory government came into power in 1874, and they practically went out in 1879. The imports and exports in 1874 were £667,000,000, but they went on decreasing until 1879, when they were £011,000,000. From 1880 to 1883 they increased till they were £732,000,000. (Applause.) He did not himself attach too much importance even to these figures, because they were based on value, but he found that from 1874 till 1879 there was a constant de- crease in the value of almost everything. The price of iron, with which he was more familiar, Came down from £lO to £ll to a little over £5 It went up in 1883, but it was now even worse than in 1879. Still the imports and exports of the country were not down to the low figure they were in 1879. (Hear, hear.) They found the total amount of money in the Post Office savings bank, and in what was called trustees' savings bank, to be in 1875, £67,000,000. in 1879 the amount stood at £75,000,000, and in 1883 at £88,000,000, so that if they considered the savings of the people they found that the country, instead of going downward, as Alderman Davies said, they found it to be greatly progressing. When they turned to the income tax they fotind that the returns in 1875 were £571,000,000, in 1879 £578,000 000. and in 1882 £llOO.OOO. (Rear, hear.) These were perhaps the beat methods they could devise for checking the course of trade and industry in this country, although be saw that Mr. Ecroyd said he did not care to trust that method. He said he preferred to believe in his own eyes and ears, and of course they could all do that, but there was such a thing as seeing what they wanted to see and bearing what they wanted to hear. He thought that was very much the condition of the Tory party. (Hear, hear.) He was afraid it was one of those things they would have to submit to, and leave them to follow in their own way. (Hear, hear.) Alderman Davies impeached free trade, and Mr. McMinnies could give them a great deal of Information about that as he at a time when protection was the order of the day, and he knew something of the poverty and misery that existed in those days. (Hear, hear.) He (the chairman) WAS only old enough to remember the end of it, and what he would say was this, that he had not the slightest desire to see the working people of this country return to such a condition of things as existed when he WAS a boy. (Hear, hear.) As far as he was able to judge, pro tection would do no one the slightest good except the land- owners. He certainly failed to see how increasing the cost of manufacturing iron could help them in their trade. (Hear, hear.)• He did see this, that if a protective deity was to be put on either pig iron, coal, or anything else it must end in one of two things, either a very large reduction in wages or the abolition of the trade altogether. (Hear, hear.) Referring to the House of Lords, he said that if any of them bad a machine which would not do its work, or somebody would not let it do its work, he did not see any harm in putting it Into proper condition, If the Tory party or any party chose that the butt of Lords should make it impos- sible to carry cettain laws they would aesist in every possible way they could in endeavouring to remove the obstruction. No amount of nonsense would hinder them from reforming the House of Lords, and if they could not reform it then they would abolish it. That was the common-sense way of dealing with it. (Applause.) Alderman Davies had made a reference to the question of the Church, and he was afraid they would think him (the chairman) an extreme man on that question. ("No, no.") lie had no feeling spinet the Episcopal Church as such. He was not a Liberatioeist, and he did not think he ever professed to be a Liberationist. But he I eould not shut his eyes to certain facts. To give an illus- tration, only the day previous in two charches, ens in War- rington god one in the neighbourhood, there were political sermons delivered from the same text," Render unto Calmar that which belongs to Caw, and unto God that which be- longs to God," (Laughter.) Every Church school in Warrington was at the service Of the Tory party; every elergymati waS att instrument al these elections in the hands of the Tory party. (Hear, hear.) While he bad no wish to disestablish and disesclow the Church without seeing what was to going to become of its funds, but if it was to make itself a tool of the Tory party then he would disestablish and disendow it. (Loud applause.) Disestablishment and disendowment of the Church would be justified because he believed its association with the Tory party would make it a danger to the interests of this country. (Applause.) Take the Church as it existed in Warrington at the present time. Take the Parish Church with all its troubles—(Mr. Broadbent: "And all its curates" and loud laugh- ter)—yes, and its seventy curates; take that end of the town, where he was told upon excellent authority that if a Sunday School teacher ven- tured to give offence to the vicar her name was struck off the list, and she was turned out of the school • take the north end of the town, where they had a church that had no light except from tallow candles' because the place was in such a disgraceful state that the Corporation would not allow them gas when he was on the Gas Committee; and then take the south end of the town, where a congregation which had worshipped for 30 or 40 years was practically driven eat because they could not conform to the will et a newly-appointed clergyman. All these things were ques- tions that perhaps affected churchmen more than anybody else, but he could not shut his eyes to the fact that they must tend to demoralise the church, and make it less effective for good than it would be if it were disestablished. (Applause.) And when Aid. Davies came down from his pinnacle of Christianity to argue with them as atheists he (the chairman) dung back his words. (Ap- plause.) He might tell Alderman Davies that the little con- gregation to which he (the chairman) belonged•and which had existed for more than 200 years, had done more for the intellectual, moral, and spiritual welfare of Warrington daring the last century than all the churches put together. (Applause.) He ventured to say that even at this day, yet they had not received one half-penny of state pay, and not one half-penny outside their own congregation, because it was a fact that although the congregation of which he spoke had been consistent in season and out of season in helping other people, there was scarcely 'one body outside Its own that had ever contributed one penny to its funds. (Rear, hear, and applause.) When Alder Man Davies talked to him about being an atheiest because he happened to differ from him and his orreligionists, it only showed how blind a man might become bY such a system when he could see no good in any church but his own little circle. (Heavy hear, and loud applause.) Wr. W. Mr. Broadbent and himself had the privilege of entering the apartment of the carriage in which Mr. Gladetone was travelling, and—he did not know whether Mr. Broadbent had noticed it or net— it was a great pleasure to see that more than once in the'brielf•conversation they had the old fire come into the we, and there was a flush which showed that there was stfil•the old vigour which they had been accustomed to, and which they all hoped would de so mach for the gauss they held. He had to re-conquer the position of power from which he was driven on the 9th June in this year, and he was going also to preach a crusade, as Peter the hermit did. (Applause.) GENERA.L NEWS. At Birmingham, on Wednesday, Lord Chitties Beresford unveiled a large obelisk erected in St. Philip's churchyard to the memory of Colonel Burnaby. A serious explosion of gas occurred at Leicester on Sun- day. The door and windows were blown out, the furniture took fire, and the occupier, named White. was very much injured. Dr. W. B. Carpenter, C 8.F.R.5.. the eminent physiolo- gist, died at three o'clock on Tuesday morning at his resi- dence, 56, Regent's- Park-road. London, from the effects of an accident sustained on Mosday. COAGIMINE.—Cement for Broken Articles, 6d. ls, 2s : postage 2nd. Sold everywhere. Kay. Bros.. Btookport.—Adtte. The Very Rev. Dean O'Loughlin visited the Catholic University. Stephen's-green, Dublin, on Monday, to cele- brate mass in the church, when he Was suddenly seized with a fit of apoplexy, and died in a few minutes. The Irish Roman Catholic bishops will not furnish the Educational Endowments Cernmission with the information sought concerning the constitution, management, and educa- tion in Irish Roman Catholic Endowed Schools. , The cotton operatives at Glasgow have consented to a compromise. The masters gave notice of a7i per cent. re- duction. This caused a strike. On Saturday the operatives agreed to commence work at 5 per cent. reduction. A Dtseereous STORM.—A storm has swept over the west coast of South America. Several towns were flooded. and a considerable quantity of nitrate was dissolved at 1 Iquique. where the damage done is estimated at $200,000. 1 As a result of the plan adopted by some East Kent farmers of killing their own fat stock and retailing the joints to the public, several cheap butchers in the town and villages are now selling shoulders of mutton at 6ci and 6i and beef at 6d to 8d per lb. WRECK AND Loss OF THIRTY-SEVEN LIVES.—The Cana- dian Pacific steamer Algona went ashore in Thunder Bay on Sunday night, and became a total wreck. The Algoma had on board 52 persons, including crew and passengers. Only 15 have been saved. The extraordinary billiard match, Peall and Mitchell, 15,000 up, at Westminster Aquarium, terminated on Satur- day night, Peall winning by 5,305. The finish was sensa- tional, Peall running out with a break of 1,150, which, on being asked te continue, he increased te 1.912, which in- cluded 634 successive spot strokes. MURDER OF AN EXPLORING PARTY —According to intel. ligence received at Melbourne, Australia, the blacks at Thursday Island report that all the members of the Geogra- phical Society's expedition to New Guinea, under General Averil, have been murdered oy natives on the Fly River. The rumour requires confirmation. Setoorrere OF AN ALLEGED Spy.—At Tamatave. Mada- gascar, the French have shot a man who was under British protection. They charged him with the offence of convey- ing information to the enemy. The Hovas are increasing their defences, and the French continue to shell them every day. The French are as suspicious of foreigners as ever, and persons are searched both on embarking and on land- ing. THE Cormier RIEL.—A New York telegram says that as the date fixed for Riel'a execution falls on Thanksgiving Day, a further respite has been granted him. The sheriffs have begun the necessary preparation at Regina. The fourth respite has created intense excitement through- out the Canadian Dominion. The French residents are jubilant and express a general belief that Riel will escape banging. A MOTHER DROWNING HERSELF AND HER Two CHILDREN.-0a Sunday, the body of Charlotte Smith was found floating in the canal. near Rawn Hill Bridge, at Ather- stone. On teeing removed from the water it was discovered that two children were tied to her. Attempts were made to restore respiration but without avail. She is sup. posed to have fastened 'dm children to her and then come ;pitted suicide. Part of the crew are negroes, and some of the men went before the magistrates and told a piti- ful tale of alleged ill-treatment at the bands of the captain and ethers of the crew. IMPORTANT CLUE TO A MURDER—The police have made a discovery in connection with the murder of a cattle dealer at Cowbridge, in the house of Edward and David Roberts, in custody on suspicion of being concerned in the reerder. It was noticed that a brick in the flre-plaCe had been recen- tly refixed and vanished. On tbis being removed about £7O was discovered. This is the amount that deceased had when murdered. TERRIBLE FATE.—A despatch from Washington. Arkan- sas, gives details of a terrible fate which has overtaken a man named Churchill, who murdered Dennis Brooks. The prisoner was confined le an old wooden building. One night a mob saturated the lower part of the building with coal•oil, and fired it. Churchill piteously begged the mob to shoot him, but the flames soon reduced the building and the victim to ashes. Loss OF £1,150 IN BANK NOTES.—The Hull police are investigating a case in which a female servant has lost £1,150 in Bank of England notes, entrusted to her care by her master. She has implicated two parties who are in a respectable position in Hull, with whom she had some drink on the evening when she missed her purse and the bank' notes. One of the gentlemen had changed a £lOO note the' number of which was known to the owner. One of ;hem hae left the town. DARING Brrnoeear.—A burglary was committed at Rye on Saturday morning by a thief, who first extinguished the gaslights in the street, and, after removing the shutters of the jewelry establishment of Mr. C. R. Allen, smashed a pane of glass and ransacked the window. Ultimately he was seen from a bedroom opposite, and on the man call. ing to the burglar he decamped with forty silver and four- teen gold watches, a quantity of wedding and keeper rings, brooches, &c., the whole worth of which Is valued at /200. MR. PARNELL AND BISHOr O'REILLY.—Mr. Parnell, Mr. T. P. O'Connor, and Mr. Kenny on Wednesday waited upon Dr. O'Reilly, the Roman Catholic Bishop of Liverpool, at the Palace, Everton. Mr. Parnell informed his Lordship that Mr. O'Connor had been adopted as the candidate for the Sc-tland Division of Liverpool. An interchange of views upon the situatiaa took plates, and at the close et the rinterview his Lordship, while carefully guarding himself against any interference with political parties, expressed 'himself heartily in favour of Me O'Connor's candidature, pleated With the views expressed by M. Parnell and his colleagues. THE Nerneelte llnnelesave--The Mayor of Carnets (Mr B. Scott) has opened a subscription to mark the public ap- preciation of the conduct of the polioe eehetables and rail. way setvants Who risked their lives in the attempt to arrest, and who finally slideettled in arresting, the three men who are 'believed to have been engaged in the jewellery robbery at Netherby, and also to raises small fund for the benefit of the Widow sod children of the murdered policeman Byrnes. --The prisoners Rudge, Martin, and Baker were formally re- manded on Saturday. On Wednesday the three men were brought before the magistrates at Carlisle. Lady Hermione Graham said the value of the jewellery in the room which was entered was about £l,OOO, and the valne of that stolen was £250. She identified as hers the eardroo fouad near the scene of one of the encounters between police and burglars. Other witnesses deposed to the prisoners' proceedings in the neighbourhood immediately prior to the robbery, including their inquiries as to the family at the Hall being at home. The prisoners were also identified by I ome of the police officers with whom they had come into conflict. LORD HARTINGTON IN ROSSINDALES.—Lord Hartington addressed a large gathering of the electors of the Rossen- dale division at Haslingden on Wednesday night. Advert- ing to the foreign policy of the present Government he ex• pressed approval of the course they were following, but said that this course was not in accord with the declarations they made in Oppoaition. Re said it was for the interest of the country that Parliament, as speedily as possible, place our whole land system upon a secure, durable, and per- manent foundation. As to the positions taken up by the moderate and adeanced Liberals, he said it was not to the advantage of the country that the Liberal party should be confined to a Radical party. It was through the mixed composition of the Liberal party that reforms which had been adopted in this country had been gradually, wisely, and safely carried. Referrirg to Lord Randolph Churchill's recent speech. he said that he would only refer for a mo- ment to the good taste of Lord Randolph in declaring that he was a party to any compact with the man Carey. who was directly concerned in carrying into execution the plot for the assassination et his (Lord Harticgton's) brother. MR. BRIGHT AT ROCHDALE.—Mr. Bright addressed a meeting held in the Circus, Rochdale, on Wednesday even- ing, in support of the candidature of Mr. T. B. Potter, MP., for the borough. Mr. Potter will be unable to take part in the election because of the death a few days ago of his wife. Between 2,000 and 3,000 people were present, and the meeting was characterised by great enthusiasm. A resolution was passed declaring unabated confidence in Mr. Gladstone and thd leaders of the Liberal party, and expres- sing an earnest hope that the voice of the people would call them again to power to effect needful reforms and guide the destinies of the people of the empire. Mr. Bright spoke in support of a resolution thanking Mr. Potter for twenty years of faithful service to Rochdale, assuring him of the deep sympathy ef his constituents in his bereavement, and adopting him as the Liberal candidate in the present elec- tion. The right hon. gentleman dealt extensively With the causes of trade depression, and showed the evil effects abroad of Lord Salisbury's utterances on the subject of protective tariffs. He urged the people of this country to look with the greatest suspicion up.n every man who would tempt them to go back a single step in the progress we bad made on this question during the last 40 years.

div.head: LIBERAL MEETING IN THE COOPERATIVE HALL.
div.p: LIBERAL MEETING IN THE CO- OPERATIVE HALL.

On Tuesday evening a crowded and enthusiastic meeting was held in the Co-operative Hall, War- rington, in support of • Mr. W. Crosfield. The chair was taken by Alderman John Crosfield, J.P., who was supported by Mr. J. Samuelson (labour candidate, Liverpool), Mr. W. Crosfield, J,P, Mr. McMinnies, M.P., Rev. J. Yonge, Dr. Gornall, Messrs. F. Monks, W. Burn, J. H. Fleming, Winser, Thorn- ton, 11. Roberts, A. Browne, and W. Diggle. For a considerable time before the commencement of the proceedings Mr. Diggle was the sole occupant of the platform. and he amused the audience by mak- ing a discursive speech, in- the course of which he touched upon all subjects, imperial and local, that are at all to the front at present. His imitation of Sir Gilbert Greenall's well known style of speaking, and his allusion to Morley Common and the fishing at Walton reservoir were particularly relished. Additional interest had been aroused by the announcement that certain fabrications put into circulation by the Tory organ would be dealt with, and this was heightened by i the fact that a hand- bill had been distributed n which it was set forth that a representative of that organ would be present to meet the charges. After Mr. Walker had made his statement, however, that represeptative if he was present did not think fit to accept the invi- tation that was given to him, second thoughts hav- ing evidently brought discretion. On the chair- man's table were placed two loaves' a large one and a small one, the former of which it was stated amidst laughter and applause was the Liberal loaf and the latter the Conservative lockf. Mr. Crosfield and his party on coming on to the platform were loudly I applauded, The CHAtrtarite, who was received with applause, said that in 1880 Sir Richard Aseheton Cross said there was a lying spirit abroad in the country, and it struck him (.fr. Crosfield) that there was a lying spirit abroad at this elec- tion. (Hear, hear.) The Tories were going about making false statements about the Liberal party. He supposed the reason was that they could not speak the truth to do them harm, and therefore they had to imagine things against them to try to knack then down. The other day his friend Alderman BraViee was speaking in the town, and he said, speaking about the two Governments. one was a Government composed of men who hod proved themselves , during the last five months able to conduct, even with a minority in Parliament. the affairs of the country with suc- cess, and the other a Government under whom they had had five years of downward ruin. The reason why the Liberal Government did not succeed in cluing more than r they did during the five years—and they did a good deal— was because of the persistent and pricked obstruction of the Tories—(hear, hear)—and the reason why the Tory Govern- ment for tire months went along so smoothly was because, , although there was a large Liberal majority in the House of Commons, the Liberals behaved themselves. (Hear, • hear.) Then he spoke of the downward ruin of those five years. Well, there were mere wages paid during those free years than in any five years since England existed. There was more money in the savings bank, there ware fewer paupers, and those were not indications, be took it, of ruin. . They were indications that the country was prcsperous. The working-classes in this country. he ventured to say, r were never so well off as they were to-day. They spoke of I trade depression, but lag would tell them what the truth was. it was depreseisn of capita. In 1873 and 1874 the trade in this country was very prosperous. Manufacturers r were making a great deal of money. There was one large ironworks in Warrington that made ever 50 per cent, of pro- fit in one of those years, and the consequence was that the • manufacturers began extending their works, and extended them to such an extent that more goods had been manufac- tured than were wanted, and hence 'there had been the de- pression of capital, but there had been no reduction of wages. The wages that were befog paid in this country were as high as ever were paid before, and the working- classes, as he previously said, ware never better off. Alder- man Davies then went on to say that he believed in free trade as enunciated by the great Men of the past. Well, be was very glad to hear him say that ranch. There were a good many Tories who were afraid to say that they were in favour of free trade, and el good many said they were in favour of free trade who were not; and if Mr. Davies be- lieved in free trade as enunciated by the great men of the past, he should like to know where there WAS a greater man or a more noble-minded patriot than John Bright. (Applause.) John Bright was as firm a free trader to-day as ever he was in his life.. They all knew, as well as he, that they owed free trade principally to to the efforts of Richard Cobden and John Bright. (Applause.) Then the Tories had tried to damage the 'Liberal party by savimg they refused to have anything to do with the commission on what they called fair trade. He called it unfair trade. (Hear, hear.) But , what was the fact? They formed s cemmission compovd entirely of Tories or fair traders, and then selected one : Liberal, like Mr. Slagg—(applause)—the member for Man- chester, and asked him to join, but Mr. Slagg very properly declined to join a commission composed in that manner, and then they asked another Liberal, like Mr. Goschen, and 'he declined for the same reason. Therefore It was not fair of those men to accuse the Liberal party of having de- clined to join a commission of that sort, when they were not going to be fairly treated, and when their assistance would have been perfectly uselese (Hear, hear ) Fair traders advocated what they called retaliatory tariffs, but Sir Robert Peel, 40 years ago, stated that that had been tried and bad failed, and therefore it was absurd to try it again now. They tried those tariffs from 1800 to 1840. The country was in a wretched state, the imports and ex- ports positively decreased, and was it likely that they were going back to a system like that—(" no ")—which bad been

WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL. ELECTION OF MAYOR. The annual meeting of this body was held in the Council Chamber of the Town Hall, on Monday, at noon. The Mayor (Alderman Harrison) presided, and there were also present Aldermen Burgess, Oros- field, Chandley, Davies, Holmes, and Webster; Coun- cillors Jolley, Litton, Broadbent, Hutchinson, Brown, Roberts, Francomb, Ashton, Barker, Bolton, Dakin, Dixon, Fleming, Greenall, Greening, Marsh, Milner, Ridgway, J. rierpoint, W. rierpoint, Pltt, Sutton, Taylor, Wright, Tinsley, and Whittle; Messrs. W. H. Brook (town clerk), J. L. Whittle (deputy town clerk), C. Chorley (borough treasurer), T. Longdinl (borough surveyor), and J. H. Gornall (medical officer' of health). Councillor &Troll proposed that Alderman Joseph Harrison be re-elected mayor for the ensuing year. He had, he said, every confidence in proposing that resolution, because, he believed, from remarks that he had heard on all aides, both in and out of the Council. that everyone desired that Alderman Harrison should be re-elected. He believed that if they succeeded in re•electing him to the office of mayor they would all have reason to congratulate themselves upon the ap- pointment. Councilor FRANCON:I3 seconded the resolution. He believed, he said, that the present mayor had fulfilled the duties incumbent upon his offiae in a way satisfac- tory to everyone in the town. He thought that Alder- man Harrison would be unanimously re-elected to ful- fill the important position of mayor Alderman Dimas supported the resolution. Re- ferring to the time when he first entered the Council, he said that he must confess that he entered it at a time when there was severe party feeling in the town, and that at that time strong party feelings were imbued in his mind. That strong feeling, which was shared by others in the Council, influ- enced them so much that he thought the town suffered to some extent in consequence. But when, in 1871, he was elected mayor, be found that the work was not one of politics at all, but one solely of carrying out the interests of the ratepayers. He found that he was supported most heartily by both political sides, and that party was 1014 entirely. In great endeavours all worked unitedly together. and, with those circumstances in his mind, he concluded never to let polities interfere with the sacred trust imposed on him. The alderman pro. °ceded to speak further on the subject, maintaining that, however they might fight politically outside, all party feelings should in that Council be forgotten. in the desire to work in the beet way for the good of the town and the ratepayers. The first duty of the Mayor would be to hold the scales of justice at the coining election. Did they mean to tell him that a creature of any political party could hold those scales properly, knowing that he was the creature of a political party P (A Voice "Yes.") He maintained that there was an independence that the Council should exercise, and they would believe him when he said that these remarks did not apply to the present Mayor. On the contrary, he had the fullest confi- dence that Alderman Harrison, whom he hoped would be elected, would do all that he had said in oarrying out the work of the Council. The resolution was then put, and carried unani. mously. The IiATOB, in reply, after subscribing the usual declaration, said that that being the third consecutive time that they had done him the honour to elect him Mayor of Warrington, he felt that he need say but little, except to return his sincere thanks for that continuation of their confidence and respect—for he must naturally assume that they were to some extent imbued with those qualities, or otherwise they could not have that day sanctioned his re-appointment. When he made his bow, as he supposed, at the last meeting of the Council, and retired from that import- ant position, he had not the slightest idea of ever being put in nomination again. He felt that, having served two years, it was as long a time as it was prudent for him to serve, and he had the greatest reluctance to stop the way against any other candi- date. He sympathised with the views of Alderman Davies that polities should not influence them in the Council, either in the selection at mayors, aldermen, or councillors, but unfortunately that state of affairs did exist. Oaly the other day he saw a long tabular statement giving the re- sults of municipal elections up and down the country, from which a deduction was made as to the probable state of political feeling at the general elee- tion. He should be glad if a truce were demanded and political feeling extinguished once and for ever. There was a time when they had no politics in the Council, but, unhappily, a change took place, and a certain number of gentlemen in the Council in those days felt that they, in point of numbers, were domi- nant, and the old shibboleth which sprung from the old aphorism, "majorities must rule," was established, and had been continued ever sinee. It was • great misfortune, but they derived • little satisfaction from the fact that, however fiercely political battles might be fought in the town, when they crooned the thres- hold of the Council Chamber they no longer knew anything about polities. (Hear, hear.) It was of the highest consequence that they should select both members of the Council and Mayors from some other feeling than that instigated by political considera- tions. No one who read the signs of the times could oloee his eyes to the feet that, whichever political party might gain the ascendancy, they were on the threshold of a material extension of the principles of self-government, and it was therefore moat important that in selecting members of the Council, they should be guided only by intellectual fitness, 'and the desire to apply themselves honestly and fearlessly to the discharge of the duties of their office. He was much obliged to them for having again conferred this honour upon him. Had he consulted his own feel- ings he should have respectfully begged to decline it, not that he did not esteem it a great privilege to be , possessed with the power and authority the position gave him, but because he knew that there were gen. tlemen in the Council pre-eminently qualified to fill the office, and he should be sorry indeed to be a stumbling block in their way. But sometimes exigences of parties arose, and circumstances transpired lby which one was led into °moaning to be placed in positions which one would, perhaps for personal reasons, otherwise not *lumpy. He could assure them that in the discharge of the duties of the office he should bear impartiality strictly in mind, and he felt sure that if he acted in that way no one could have the slightest hesitation in approving of the course that he should pursue. He should be extremely sorry if he ever gave the slightest reason for any one to say that anything like partiality had marked any incident in his official career. ri The Melon then nominated Alderman John Croft- field as Deputy Mayor, and the Rev. M. Gskutimt Maras, of Earlestown, has succeeded in passing the scholarship examinations held in the various colleges throughout England in July last, and becomes entitled to enter Chester Training College for Schoolmasters early in February next. He served his apprenticeship. as a pupil teacher in Billinge National Schools under Mr. Harry Williams, and since then has been assistant - master in the National Schools, Pemberton. At the same examination he also &stained second class in religious knowledge. A FOOLIiII Wouall.—Jane Gill, a tramp hailing from Eccles, near Manchester, was charged with drunken- ness under singular circumstances, at the Newton Town Hall, on Wednesday, hefcre Mr. T. J. Gillespie.—P.S. Cam.. mins informed the magistrate that on the previous evening the prisoner knocked at the door of the police station, and wished to be admitted. He advised her to go away, but she replied that she wanted a night's lodgings. She was told the police station was not a lodging-house, and after some persuasion she went away. A short time afterwards, how- ever, she was found lying drunk and incapable in the road with a crowd of 100 people round ker.—She was fined 5e and wee, or seven days' imprisonment. •

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.

LONDON, THURSDAY. The magnitude of Mr. Gladstones personal in- fluence in politics was never more strikingly illustrated than at the present juncture. Through dreary weeks we have had a succession of speeches from politicians and statesmen of more or less eminence, Mr. Chamberlain has seized the oppor- tunity of making a long advance in his career, and has established a position from which it would be difficult to dislodge him. Lord Randolph Churchill has made many speeches, shewing a woeful falling off in that rollicking humour, which was the prin- cipal recommendation of his oratory. Lord Hart- [ingon has excited some flush of interest from the desire to know what position he would take up in view of Mr. Cliamberlain's declaration. Lord Salis- bury has also made one or two, speeches at great length. But the world is weary of them, and I doubt whet4r many of the coluranslave been read
has

through. But when Mr. Gladstone appeared upon the scene everything was changed. His coming was waited with increasing interest, and I hear that the sale of the London papers on the two days when they have had reports of his speeches in Edinburgh has considerably increased. The speeches themselves, as far as they have gone, have not fallen short of expectation. MY: Gladstone speaks with an authority that no one else can assume. Mr. Cham- berlain, withhis' 'Sharp incisive sentences and his audacious assumption of right to frame a pro- gramme for the Liberal party, vanishes into the distance, and there is only Mr. Gladstone's figure left looming on the scene. in his first address de- livered immediately.on his arrival in Rdinburgh s'an Monday night, Mr Gladstone added a weighty con- tribution to political knowledge. He announced that one of the principal duties of the new Parlia- ment under the Liberal Ministry will be to concede all the just and moderate demands of Ireland for local government, always bearing in mind the prime necessity of maintaining intact the interests of the Empire. HIS declaration, contrasting fav- ourably with Lord Salisbury's not too fervid de- liverances on the point, and with Lord Randolph Churchill's :significant silence, has given satisfac- tion- not only in Liberal but in Conservative circles. Mr. Oladstone in his two speeches on Monday and Wednesday has sketched a full programme for the new Parliament with great skill and vigour and has I met the not less skilful endeavour of the Conservatives to make capital out of the apprehensions of church- 'men. Ilia emphatic declaration that the Scotch Disestabliibment question would not be dealt with in the new Parliament, still less the English ques- tion, should make an end of the idle fears of the ehurchman-first-and-Liberal-after section of the party whose hesitation is carefully fostered by Tory agents. There is enough work for the next Parlia- ment to perform without touching . a question on which the constituencies have not been specially consulted. There is what Mr. Gladstone called the "relations of the people with the land," which is presumed to refer to small holdings. There is—it is to be 'hoped this will be dealt with firdt—reform I 'of Parliamentary procedure ; and there is the great question of Local Government with its generous application to Ireland, under the reserve of imperial I interests which Mr. Gladstone put in the forefront of his statement. If the new Parliament cleals'Anc- , cessfully with these' questions• it will surely', find , enough to supply labour for a moderately long life: The Armstrong case came to a close on Tuesday night, leaving Mr. Stead in prison, arrayed in a loose-fitting short jacket, a rough light-yellow material, a yellow glengarry-shaped cap, and trousers of a loose baggy yellow linen of the "duck " type, striped with the Government airw in ink in four different places. His bootsewere Made to fit some other criminal. Ile is -Mr:stead no longer, but number something or other, set forth in a round cloth label sewn onto the left breast of his jacket. This is a picture told in the words of the Rev. M. Waugh, who has had, an interview with Mr. Stead. Many an interview has the editor of the Tall Mall Gazette planned and directed, but it never occurred to him that he himself would come to be interviewed in this condition. The sentence passed upon him of. three months, albeit without hard labour, goes far beyond general ex- pectation. He was found guilty by the jyry, and it was necessary that some punishment should fol- low. But the general sense of the public, excluding the section who have from the first pursued Mr. Stead with implacable vindictiveness, is that the sentence is unduly severe. 'Without hard labour," Mr. Justice Lopes said. But surely he would not think it, apart from the degraded associations of the task, an absence of hard labour to pick a pound of oakum a day? This Mr. Stead has to do, upon a breakfast taken at six o'clock. of skilly and brown bread, a. dinner of suet-pudding and brown bread, and a supper. at half-past five of the inevitable' skilly and brown bread. Toujours perdriz would be ' a luxury after this. The evening meal is the best of the day. For more than twelve hpura: the pri- soner has nothing to eat. This is a simple story that cannot fail to defeat the ends of justice, and ' raise a howl of indignation. No one would defend lir. Stead's mode of action. He is not a wise man. 3ut he is an honest man who has done conspicuous service to morality, and this is not the treatment for honest men, however misguided. The Court at Balmoral is beginning tO pack up preparatory for the flight southward. This will be a movement that will be hailed with joy by all the Court, who, owing to the weather, have had a ter- ribly bad time of it this year. None will be more pleased than Prince Henry of Battenberg, for whom a special torture has been invented'. The Queen insistikupon his appearing upon all public occasions in Scottish costume, which for the beginner may be well enough in July or August, but is a sore trial in November. The unhappy prince Was thus attired on the occasion of the opening of the Ballater Bridge .2 day, and an eye-witnesawhas printed a account of the Prince with chattering teeth look as if he rather liked the kilt. One the most lamentable aspects of the question is i the absence of human sympathy in these trying cir- cumstances. There is a general disposition to be- , lieve that the Prince made a bargain with his eyes open, and he is now left to take the consequences with that cheery feeling with which we are enabled to view the discomfiture of our fellow-men. . Mr. Labouchere views with a light hart the tremendous action for libel which is brought against him by Mr. Alderman Harris, of Dublin. The alder- man claims .£lO,OOO damages, and Mr. Labouchere hopes he may get it. I forget what is the precise charge against the proprietor of Truth in the case of the Alderman; but it cannot be so serious as that alleged in the case of a Spanish grandee—the Duke of Vallambrossa I think it was—who two , years ago brought an--action against Truth, laying damages at a similar sum. I remember asking Mr. Labouchere what were-the grounds of thealleged libel. "Oh." he answered, we only said that his great grandfather had been an army contractor in the time of the First Napoleon, and had acquired much wealth by potting the corpse found on the field of battle and serving the compound up to their surviving comrades in the form of rations." That was all; but it seemed almost enough. The Duke lost the case because it was ruled by the judge that an action for libel could not ibe n the case of a long dead grandfather. It remains to be seen how Alderman Harris will .prosper. Mr. Labouchere, though pursuing an apparently reckless course in Truth, generally manages to keep on the safe side, as is testified to by the fact that he has never yet been cast in damages. One result of the present great depression' in trade and unemployment of every kind is showing itself in a determination to expel the foreigner. During the period Of our "unexampled eemmercial prosperty " many branches of trade slipped from tite hands of Englishmen, and were eagerly availed of by artisans and artificers of other countries. Thus the watch trade employs and supports a whole colony of Swiss who have settled down at Clerken- well. Much of the good old English Chippendale furniture is made by Frenchmen in Soho, while the restaurant trade is largely in the hands of Italians. These colonies of foreigners have existed in London for decades, in some instances for centuries. For instance the French colony at Soho owed its origin to the revocation of the Edict of Nantes. , There was room for all and work for all. The company of which the new Lord Mayor is master is certainly not a poor one, and if the leather- sellers made their money by selling leather, one branch of trade would at all events be safe from the influences of depression. The leather-sellers are given to hospitality, and spent last year £795 on wine, tbeir whole expenditure in keeping up the in- stitution, paying salaries and singers, and enter- taining amounted to £lB,OOO. Even the humble beadle strikes oil when he touches a civic salary. Three hundred a year does not seem very much con- templated from a city point of view, but then there are the pickings and the perquisites. City beadles, are better paid than country rectors.

THE EN AMINEit SATURDAY. NOVEMBER 14, 1885.

- LIBERAL NIEETING AT RUNCORN. SPEECH BY MR. BRLTNNER. liesda Lecture Hall was crowded on Wednes- day evening by an enthusiastic audience, gathered to support the candidature of Mr. J. T. Brunner. Mr. James Handley, J.P.' presided, and he was Sup- ported on the platform by the candidate; the Revs. J. D. Thomas and Hugh Gilmour; Messrs. J. R. Frith, S. Taylor, B. Kniveton, T. E. Ellis, 0. Leak, C. Littler, W. Handley, and S. C. Beckett. The CRaintaaN said he felt it was his duty to thank those present for assembling in such strong force. They were met once more in support of the cause of Liberalism, which they believed to be best for their interests, and for the couotry at large. Trust in the people being the cardinal principle of Liberalism, they had nothing to conceal, and these meetings were called that they might be fully in- formed upon the great questions of the day, and the aims and policy of the Liberal party. (Applause.) The Rev. J. D. THOM&S moved the following resolution : "That this meeting hailit with delight the visit of Mr. Gladstone to Midlothian—(cheers)—and trusts that he will be returned to power at the head of a united and triumphant majority—(cheere)—with Mr. Brunner amongst the number. (Loud cheers.) Mr. Thomas said they felt sure that the banner which Mr. Gladstone bad unfurled waf the banner under which the people would range themselves —(hear, hear)—and that the leader who conducted the Liberal party to victory in 1880 was also the leader who would lead them to a greater victory in 1385. (Applause.) The resolution contained the word "trust." The man who trusted was the man who worked. (Hear, hear.) We showed our faith by our works—(hear, hear)—and he felt confident that if those present that night would only do their utmost they would see Mr. Brunner amongst the number of Mr. Gladstone's majority. (Applause.) Mr. B. Kerrerrow seconded the resolution, which he be- lieved they would see translated into a fact. He advised them to do their best to break the back of Toryism in Cheshire, and to vote straight for Mr. Brunner. The Tories were quite conscious that they were playing a losing game, and were moving almost heaven and earth for an election wry. They began with poor Gordon, but we heard nothing about him now. They had been to India, Egypt, and Africa for an electioneering cry, and nothing had succeeded yet. (Applause.) Now they were turning their attention to Fair Trade and free education' and hoped by these to catch the votes of the few hundred working-men who happened to be suffering from depression in trade. They had tried Protection, and knew what it did for them—emptying everybody's stomach and pockets as well. The food of the country and almost every other article was 50 per cent cheap-r than it was before Free Trade came into operation, and were they to go back to those days of Protection. (Applause.) He pointed out how Frei Trade operated bene- ficially to England, and said the more we did with foreign nations, the more they would do with us. (Applause) Al- luding to free education, Mr. Kniveton said there was not a working-man or child in England that would not benefit l-ar It, and the coun,ry would be made happy and prosperous, and more free from crime. (Loud applause.) The Rev. Hunt GILMOUR made an admirable speech ,In support of Mr. Brunner's candidature, and dwelt in an elo- quent fashion upon the legislation of the Liberal party in the past, and the measures of amelioration the people might expect from them in the future. ' Mr. J. D. JOWES also supported the resolution. Mr. Brunuer, he said, had made use of words at reat Budworth which deserved to be written in letters of living light. They were—" I want to spend my life in the abolition of pau- Perism." (Cheers.) Party politics were right in their way, but if this country was to be elevated from the slough into which it had got social politics must be paid more attention to than they bad been. When we remembered that accord- ing to the registrar general's returns one in every fifteen of the inhabitants of the United Kingdom died in a work- houee, It was, he thought, a matter that somebody ought to look into. and be was highly delighted that Mr. Brunner bad taken op as his life's work the abolition of pauperism. It was a noble resolve on the part of any human being—(applause)—becouse it was a determination to lighten and brighten the lot of the seething masses arocnd us. (Applause.) Mr. Terdin at a public meeting recently I held seemed to be greatly concerned that the teetotallers of the division were not going to vote for a fellow teetoller. Mr. Verdin cried out before he was hurt. It was only that very night that the temperance delegates had decided upon the question of which candidate was to receive their support, and they had come to the unanimous decision that Mr. Brunner was the man to receive their votes. (Load ap- plause.). Mr. Verdin must think that teetotallers were not tbinkera. • At all events he could not give them credit for much sensate imagine that they were going to support him because be was a teetotaller. Lord Salisbury might claim the support of non-smokers because he did not smoke him- self, and for the matter of that Mr. Chamberlain might claim Mr. Verdin as one of his supporters because he weate an eye glass. (Laughter.) The teetotallers were not going I to he caught with such blind chaff ae that. He (Mr. Jones) I had been a member of the United Kingdom Alliance since 1871, and be was rather too old at that game, when they came to the teetotallers upon the legislative aspect of tem- perance. They wanted a man who would vote for local option, and if a man had been 36 years considering the question he must he a very dell man er there most be some other object in view if he could not come to a decision. Mr. Verdin evidently wanted to secure the votes of the pub- lican and the teetotallers, but a man that gaited the publi- cans did not suit the teetotallers. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Brunner was in unison with the teetotallers on local option, and they bad passed the following resolution:—" That this meeting of temperance delegates having heard tbe report of the deputation which waited upon the candidates for the Northwich Division of Cheshire, strongly recommends tem- perance electors of this division to support Mr. Brunner's candidature, and urges them to use every legitimate effort to secure his return at the coming election." (Ap- plause.) Mr. T. E. Erns, of Northwich, also addressed the meet- ing upon the achievements of the Liberal party, and made some remarks, which he said were good unadulterated Radicalism, to his fellow countrymen, in Welsh. The resolution was carried enthesiasticaliy and unani- mously. Mr. BRUNNER, who was received with continued cheer. leg, said at that late hour, he was not going to make any- thing like an eloquent speech, but be should like to touch upon two or three subjects that bad been named that night, and he hoped to be able to give them some illustrations that as sensible, clearheaded men, as they had been described, weuld enable them to meet some of the arguments of the Tories. They had been told that we seemed according tta trade returns to be getting into England a great deal more? than we were selling, so that we always had a balance and were getting poorer. (Laughter.) He would explain to them by a simple illustration how it appeared that goods coming into the country were more in value than the goods going out. A ton of Coal left Newcastle-on-the-Tyne and it was entered into the Custom-house book at 9m. It went to San Francisco in an English shin at a cost of 15s for freight; therefore when it got to San Francisco it was Worth 248..1 That 24s would buys quarter of wheat, and that wheat put on board the same ship came back to Liverpool. But there was 1.5 s more freight added to it, making the value of the quarter 39e, so that we got 39s for our 9s. And did we owe a clipper to anybody for it ? (Applause.) All the difference was due to Englishmen for their work—for the value of the ship and the wages of the seamen, and they did rot owe anything at all. (Applause.) He world give them an illustration Of the extreme danger of going in for protection, and it should be an illustration that a very large number of men would understand. He was an alkali maker by a process that he and his friends at Winnington worked alone in this coun- try. They did not use any sulphur ore ; and every otter alkali maker in the kingdom used sulphar ore to a large amount. A great many of them would remember that they had sulphur ore coming from Ireland 24 years ago. Recen- tly there was a discussion at the Town Council of Dublin as to whether they should buy their setts from an Irish quarry or from a Welsh quarry. It was advice not thickly veiled from Mr. Par- nell that the Irish people should put a duty upon setts coming from Wales for the protection of the Irish in- dustry. :Now he (Mr. Brunner) was firmly convinced that a policy like that would ruin Ireland, and very sadly dam- age England. This being the spirit in which Mr. Parnell approached trade questions what would he do when he came to consider the abandoned sulpher ore mines of Ireland. He would try to—he gave hina credit for being a thoroughly honest, patriotic man—(hear, hear, and aoplause)—he would try to induce a large number of men in the House of Commons—Englishmen as well as Iriehmen—to join him in this policy. Amongst the Tories there were a very large number of men who were hankering after this policy—(hear, hear)—and 80 men it was said were going to follow Mr. Parnell. A large number they were told were going to follow Lord Salisbury, and honest James Lowther, and Mr. Chaplin in their careers. (Laughter.) These two forces would come together and it might be that they would be nearly half of the lieuee of Commons, and that there would only be four or fire votes wanted to turn the scale and make a majority in favour of putting a heavy import duty upon sulphur ore coming from Spain. What would happen. It a heavy duty was put upon the sulphur ore every alkali works in Widnes, St. Helens, Newcastle-on- Tyne, and Glasgow, would have to pay a great deal more for the ore, and every manufacturer would find that his salt cake, soda ash, crystals, and bi-carbonate would cost a great deal more than they did before. How was it going to be with him (Mr. Brunner). If there were five votes wanted to turn the scale, and put a duty upon sulphur ore coming from Spain or elsewhere, he could afford to pay £20,000 mpiece for these votes, to get a majority, and be should make half a million a year. (Cheers.) Mind this, that if they once started upon this miserable game of protection they would bring P. about that every member of Parliament would go to the House of Commons, not for the benefit of the country. but for the sake of his own miserable pocket. ( A pplastse.) He wanted to keep trade questions out of the contest ; let them fight on political questions. (Hear, hear, and applause.) All through the discussion in which they had been engaged he had been an advocate for the freedom of the schools ' - and he did not begin when this contest began. He had been an advocate for the freedom of the schools ever since he had been art ad- vocate for anything at all. (Hear, hear.) He wished for the freeaom of schools for the reason that the rich and the poor would go to the same schools. (Hear, hear.) As a member of Parliament—he believed he should be One— (loud cheers)—he was not going to keep the sweets for the rich and the dry crusts for the poor. (Hear, hear.) He was

THE LATE MR. THOMAS NORMAN, OF RUNCORN. A special service of remembrance for the death of.the late Mr. Thomas Norman was held on Sunday night at St. Paul's Wesleyan Chapel, Runcorn. The interior was ap- propriately draped in black, and the congregation was a very large one. The preacher was the Rev. George Wood, su- perintendent minister of the circ It, who took for his text the first three verses of the 14th chapter of St. John. The rev. gentleman said the two great facts of faith embodied in the text made the life and death of our dear departed friend, the late Mr. Thomas Norman, what they were, a life of activity and benevolence, a death of exalted triumph and sacred joy. He believed in God and in Jesus Christ with all his heart, and when the call to depart came he was ready for his mansion in his Father's house. Mr. Thomas Norman woe a Christian of a practical, rather than of an emotional type. Accustomed from early life to activity, he carried his energy into every department of life, and lived. to reap the fruits of his industry and toil. He was ajnatt of pronounced individuality—.-he thought for himself-a-,And- of an indomitable will, which carried him through every ob- stacle in the attainment of his object. Kind in disposi- tion, he lived for others rather than himself, and Iby his quiet and unobtrusive generosity to the poor of I this town he won their affection and gratitude. As a pub- ' lie man Mr. Norman had fixed opinions and principles from which he never wavered, and he never hesitated to avow them when eccasion called or necessity arose. As a Town Commissioner, a Guardian of the Poor, a membar of the School and Burial Boards, he was honoured and trusted by his fellow townsmen, and he filled those posts with hon- our to himself and advantage to the town. In all Christian and rhilanthrepic enterprises he took a prominent and use- ful part. As President of the Young Men's Christian As- aociation, he greatly endeared himself to its members, with whom he had been associated for many years. TIM) temperance cause had in him an earnest and consistent worker, and like all good men he mourned ever the evils of intemperance and excese. Be could face a difficulty, finan- cial or practical, with a hero's courage, but he loved peace for its own sake. Brusque and outspoken in all his' utterances, but with a kindly, generous heart, he was ever ready to forgive, and he loved to he forgiven; and the wisdom which is from above had in him a living em- bodiment, first pure, then peaceable, gentle, easy to be en- treated, full of mercy, without partiality and without hypocrisy. Mr. Norman was a Methodist by birth and by' conviction. A member of our church, geeing a brief inter- val, for 40 years, his religious sympathies all clustered around the church of his choice. though not in any bigoted lor sectarian spirit. He loved his own community, but, as the funeral testified, his worth and influence were acknow- ledged by all the other churches of the town which were represented on that solemn occasion. He was never prominent in any of the more spiritual exercises of the church, but be always toek an active part in its material and financial prosperity, and nobly contributed and col- lected in behalf of its several Lands. Three years ago he was chosen circuit stosard for this circuit, and he is the .first who during the term of office passed away. Brought by this appointment into close relationship with the ministers, his judgment and generosity have been both highly appreciated. He was a genuine ministers' friend, and had no higher ambition than to make them happy, and the circuit, whore steward be was, prosperous and success- ful. Struggling with an insidious disease for several months, Mr. Norman continued to attend to his various and numerous duties until a fortnight prior to his death. It then became my melancholy pleasure to visit him daily 'until the end came. When the physician had declared the ease hopeless, and everything that human skill and kind- I nese could qietate had been done to prolong his life, but without avail, a new phase of his religious character seemed suddenly to develop. It illumined every interest in his public, social, and religious life. With a kind of super- natural attraction, he gathered those interests around him, reconciling differences, dictating his wishes, and providing for the filling up of the offices of the church which his death would render vacant. A glow of sacred feeling found expreseion in hymns of praise and in fervent prayer, and the numerous visitors to his bedside felt that their visits were indeed a means of grace. Eternity alone will determine and disclose the result of some of those interviews. As the end drew near he became through weakness less able t) converse, but he retained his consciousness to the last. Be was heard to say repeatedly, "Trusting, trusting, trusting." Then calmly the spirit fled to join the multitude which no man can number, whispering the name of one of his de- parted friends as it winged its way to the mansions of our Father's house. Oh, brethren, may you and I and all whom we love find our borne in that Heaven when oar work is finished, and se be " for ever with the Lord." At the close of the service the choir sang the anthem " The Vital Spark." •

FREEMASONRY.—The annual installation meeting of the Cholmondeley Lodge' No. 1.908, which took place at the Commercial Hotel, Frodsharn, was eminently successful. After the transaction of the ordinary business, the ceremony of installing Bro. J. J. Radford as W.M. was commenced by the retiring W.M,, the greater portion of the ceremony being performed by Bro. James Salmon, P.P'G.D , and treasurer for the newly-formed province of North Wales. Various officers were invested. At the conclusion of business the brethren dined, under the presidency of the W.M.. Bro. J. J. Rad fend. POPULAR CONCERT.—The first of the Frodsham popular concerts, organised and inaugurated by Mr. 'antes Kent, took place in the l'syn Hall on Tuesday evening. Thera was a large and appreciative audience. The principals were Miss Lucy A. Jones, of the Liverpool concerts, soprano ; Mr. J. F. Stuart, baritone ; Mr. Josef Cantor, hurnourist ; and Mr. R. W. Pierpoint, solo cornet. "My dearest heart" and "Let me dream again" (Sullivan) were the contri'utions of Miss Jones, who succeeded in winning a deserved recall on each occasion. In conjunction with Mr. Stuart, Miss Jones also sang a duet. Mr. Stuart, who has a capitsl baritone voice, made a favourable impression by his singing of "The wolf" and " Niatreth." He and Mr. J. Kent sang the duet " Army and navy ' in admirable style. Mr. Josef Cantor made his first appearance in Frod- sham, and WAS At once established a favourite. His efforts were each encored. Mr. Pierpoint performed two cornet solos with the skill and ability, that always distinguishes him. Not the least pleasing feature sf the concert was the glee rendered by a carefully selected choir of 19 voices. which under the conductorship of Mr. Kent, acquitted it- self in a most creditable manner. Mrs Heywood ably offi- ciated as accomoanist. Mr. Kent deserved all praise for securing such a musical treat for the Frodsham public.

He was perfectly eatisfied that if the schools were mule free, that they would have the rich and poor going together, because there never was a school made free but the rich people sent their children there. (Laughter.) It did not matter, and never would matter, who gave money for a school—how tightly it was tied up and 6011 strongly expressed their intention that it was to be a school for the poor, it was very soon filled with the rich. (Hear, hear, and laugh- ter, and a voice : " Robbed the poor of it.") They had. It was now more than 300 years since the majority of the grammar schools of this country were founded by good and Christian people, and until very recent times these schools had been free. And they could not find a poor man's child Sir,—Allow me to pass a brief remark upon one or two it g ring mis-statements made by the above gentleman and one of them from one end to another. (Hear, hear.) The ; education was always kept to such subjects as were of no use to a poor man's child. There was a grammar school the Conservatives were not opposed to the passing of the not long ago at Witton, which was now part of the Local Board district of Northwich. That was free until 30 years ; agitation ago, and the master would not have any boys there but MR H. TOLLEMACHE AT KINGSLEY. la his supporters whilst addressing the electors. One was that I Franchise. Were they not? Did they not say during the before that bill passed, through Lord Randolph 1 Churchill, that the agricultural labourer was not sufficiently rich men's boys. So it had been from one end of the country ; educated in politics to be entrusted with it, and that he was to the other. THE FALLACIES OF SIR RICHARR CROSS. Sir,—With many others I was present at the Conservative meeting held in the Viaduct Institute on Saturday last in support of Sir R. A. Cross's candidature, and I regret the slight disturbance which occurred, though it cannot be doubted by any who were present at the meeting that it was far more owing to the indiecreet zeal of the Tory officials— some of whom made themselves conspicuous by their foolish officiousness—than by anything said or done by the Liberal element. However, my object is to deal with the candidate and his views rather than with the small fry of the party. In his speech Sir R. Cross endeavoured to defend his party and himself as to the course they took in connection with the 'dorm Bill of last year. But lam afraid even so good a ial pleader as Sir Richard seems to be must have felt ti overwhelming evidence against both himself and his party. The country is too well acquainted with the action of the Tory party, and divined their motives tea accurately in this matter to be now gulled into the conviction that they were ever friendly to the measure of Reform introduced by Mr. Gladstone's Government. The country remembers too well how it met with the bitterest opposition at their bands, and that no dodge was considered too mean to enable them to defeat the hill. We also know how futile it would have been for Mr. Gladstone in the face of such an opposition te couple with the Franchise Bill a Redistribution Bill, con- sidering it was not until nearly the end of the sesaion—the month of July—that the first measure could be got through the }lnure of Commons. It is also a matter of history hew contemptuously tbe House of Lords dealt with the measure But at this point the peeiale came forward with no uncertain voice, and spoke out their demands for enfranchisement. And so loud was this voice, and so strong the determination to have this measure of justice conceded to them, that after a full measure of blustering on the part of Lord Salisbury and his followers, even the stubbornness of the House of Lords was eventually overcome. These are facts so well I known that it would be needless to repeat them, were they not now so shamelessly denied by the very party who BO consistently and furiously opposed step by step the very Measure which to-day gives so many of us the right to elect our own representative in the next Parliament. But let uil hope that on the 30,h inst. it will .be shown that all their, denials have been received at their true value, and the " big 1 thumping lies" thrown back into the faces of those who have uttered them Sir Richard went on to deal more or less satisfactorily with other subjects. eventually landing himself on the—.to him—rock of Free Education, and on this question he vainly endeavoured to throw duet in the electors eyes by laying that there could no "Free Education," and that even if school fees were done away with, that the people would still have to pay for the educatims of the young by their rates or taxes. This every intelligent voter knows full well, but he also knows that two-thirds of the cost of education is paid now by the State, and wonders why so Much opposition to the remaining third. Then again, Sir Richard feared the working man by re- ceiving free edecation for his children would lose his self- respect, even though be paid his quota of rates and taxes. If this were true. we must all deplore that he has already lost two-thirds of the quantity he ought to possess. But to the unsophisticated mind it does not appear why the self- respect of the working man should be of a more vanishing .Commodity than that of the middle classes. These have long enjoyed Free Education in Paco's, tbe endowments of which were distinctly given for the benefit of the poor. I do not know whether they have lost their self-respect by receiving their education free in schools whose funds have heen misapplied on their behalf. But Ido know that they have certainly lost none of their arrogance and conceit. It is an open secret, admitted by all, that the endowments left to our Free Grammar Schools were originally. intended for the poor of the district in which they are situated. But whorl are the sons who receive the education given in these schools. Are they the sons of the poor working man for whose benefit they were intended? Are they the eons of the poor for whom the benefactors of ages gone by intended , them, in languaee so distinct, that it becomes downright robbery on the nut of those whose sons are educated there, Ito place them there. Sir Richard Cross certainly paid the working man an unintentional compliment when he spoke thus of their self-respect, for ha admitted thereby a jealousy on their port for self-respect which is not recognised in the classes above them in the social scale. Sir Richard endeavoured to strengthen his opposition to granting Free Education, by saving it would be just as reasonable to impose upon the State the cost of feeding and clothing of our children. For, this argument he has to thank Mr. Goschen-and for how many arguments are the Tories in- debted to him. But no reasonalele mind can perceive the least analogy between the two questions. The State does not, nor never bee undertaken the slightest responsibility in the feeding and clothing of our children—at all events not of the working-man who is not a pauper—of others better- favoured I admit it does. The State does not step in be- tween parent and child and say what kind of food the former must simply the latter, hut in the matter of education it does. The came with regard to clothing. We must not lose sight of the fact that the State compels us to conform with its educational requirements. Therefore, it ought to pay the cost. The State compels vaccination, but in that instance it bears the cost. Why not also the cost of educa- tion, which is also compulsory? There are mans ether points to which I should like to refer, but soace forbids.' I will only mention the sneer of the canaiddt- in reference to the "three acres and a cow." Ho spoke as though we were wishful to have a law enacted to force a lahemer to take up the allotments What we do want is a law an enable him to do so. But his remarks on this enestion were such as might have been exPected —I am, dic., BRYTHON.

COLONEL McCono,ronAtat's MFM TING s.—Colonel McCorquodale, the Liberal candidate for the New- ton Division, is prosecuting his campaign with great vigour, and present appearances are certainly in his favour. Another series of meetings have been arranged, as will be seen from our advertising columns. To-day (Saturday), a large Liberal meet- ing will be held in the Viaduct Institute, Earles- town ; on Monday night, there will be a meeting at Great Sankey; Tuesday night, at Billinge and Moss Bank; Wednesday night, at the Volunteer Hall, St. Helens; Thursday, at Park Lane; and on Satur- day, at Croft and Padgata.

Sir,—Those who sympathise wall Mr. Stead and who be- lieve he has done so very much for the protection of those who cannot help themselves, will, I trust, do all they can to have at the door of their respective church and chapel, a petition to receive signatures asking for his immediate re- lease; also Mr. Jacques and even Mrs Jarrett. lam glad to hear that one Christian Young Men's Class in the town t has already passed a vote of sympathy.—Yours. &c. WIDNES ELFCTION SONG. MARCIE, BOYS, MARCIL Air: Tramp, tramp. 0 ye lovers of the right, Get ye ready for the tight, And away with him who dare not face the storm Think upon your sires of old; And be resolute and bold, While you strike a blow for Freedom and Reform. CHORUS. March, boys, march to meet the Tories; Moss he is nowhere in the fray. There's a champion in the field, And he does not mean to yield— Edmund Muspratt is the man to win the day. Now we've got the vote at last, Let us not forget the past; • We must tell the Tories that they plead in vain. Since the vote came from the Rads, On the polling day, my lads, We mast let the Liberals have it back again. March, boys, march, &c. We can spare young Edwards-Moss, For we shouldn't feel the 'loss If he never more should come upon the scene. For a power in the State, We must have a man of weight, And you know that MOM is light and very green. March, boys march, &c. . . We must send to Parliament One who'll truly represent ',ll‘. - v.l • Every section with a feeling for his kind.;-, One who wants to see fair play, s'. And who doesn't block the way— "" Ile must be a man of merit and of mind. March. boys, march, &c.-'4, • 0 A; We have got a righteous cause; What we want is equal laws, And the "Grand Old Man" put in his proper place; We are gaining strength each hour, While the foe is losing power— We are fighting for the freedom of the race. March, boys, march, &c. - —ED. Ex.

MR. MUSPRATT AT ITUYTON. Mr. E. K. Mus Pratt, the Liberal candidate for the Widnes Parliamentary Division, on Wednesday evening addressed a crowded meeting of his friends and supporters in Huyton and B,oby Schools, Huy- ton. Mr. Muspratt met with a very enthusiastic re- ception. He was met at Roby by the Whiston brass band, arid escorted through Huyton to the place of meeting, which was decorated with mottoes "Honest foreign policy," " Muspratt and the working-men," "Muspratt and justice to Ireland." Mr. Alexander Eccles presided, and there were also on the platform, in addition to the candidate, Messrs. William Oulton, J. Holbrook Gaskell, W. B. Bowring, T. Brocklebank, jun., T. S. Timmis, jun., E. Carey, C. S. Aldrich, H. B. Shores, and others. Mr. E. K. Muepratt, who was received with loud cheers, referred to the subject of local government coupled with [local option, saying that he believed that the sale of alco- holic liquors and the licensing of public-houses should be to the hands of the people. (Apolaase.) He wished to repeat what he had already said—that he thought education ought to be gratuitous. He wuuld also support a Royal commission of iequiry into the working of the Education Acts of 1870 and 1876. (Hear, hear.) The question of the disestablishment of the Church, he contended, ought not to and would not come before the next Parliament. The best friende of the Church were the Liberals. (Applause.) Speaking particularly to the miners of the district, he said he would certainly support Mr. Burt's bill for the amend- ment of the Employers' Liability Act. He was in favour of miners or their relatives having a voice at the inquests of people who had been killed in the 'nines; and, in fact, he said he was in favour of many of the points contended for by the miners, although he had not been asked to answer any questions. (Applause.) Having criticised the opinions held by Lord Salisbury on free trade, he went on to advocate technical education in this country. (Hear, hear.) He con- tended that it was the object of the Liberal party to see that the present land laws, with their many injustices, were amended. (Applause.) The Agricultural Holdings Act, which was passed by the Tories, was no use, because the landlords could contract themselves out of it, and it was not until the Liberals came into power that that Act was made compulsory. The tenant farmers were now more secure than in bygone days, huts great deal more had yet to be done. (Applause.) The Liberals wished to improve trade by encouraging work and reducing taxation on such articles as sugar, tea, and coffee ; bat the Tories pretended that they would improve trade by imposing various restric- tions on it. (Applause.) On the motion of Mr. C. S. Aldrich, seconded by Mr. Gerrard. and supported by Mr. William Oulton. tn sup- porting the resolution, Mr. J. A. Doughan (Catholic) said that he would follow in the steps of his colleague on the Liverpool School Board, that staunch Liberal, John Yates, as Mr. Muspratt was in favour of putting religions educa- tion on an equal footing with free schools. He prophesied from the reception the candidate received a great sucoess, but they must work and conduct the election on the broadest lines. A vote rif confidence in the candidate was passed, and the proceedings terminated with a vote of thanks to the chairman. The band escorted Mr. Muspratt to the station, crowds following And cheering all the way. MR. MUSPRATT AND THE RAILWAY SERVANTS. The Secretary of the Widnes Branch of the Railway Ser- vants' Society has forwarded the following list of questions to both candidates for the Widnes Division : I —Are you in favour of the renewal of the Employers' Liability Act and its amendments, as proposed by the Bill of Mr. T. Burt, M.P.? 2.—Are you in favour of conferring on the Board of Trade power to compel the Railway Calm:moles to adopt an efficient continuous automatic brake on all passenger trains, and an efficient braltn for goods and mineral trains ; an improved method of coupling railway vehicles, which would not necesaitate men going between them for this purpose; an efficient system of block signalling, and a periodic,i return of railway servants engaged in working the traffic who are kept or allowed to be on duty more than 12 hours out of every 24? 3.—Will you recommend the Board of Trade to increase the system of inspection of Railways, by appointing practi- cal railway men as sub-Inspectors, with a view of prevent- ing accidents to the men employed on them, and the travel- ling public ? ill you support the Bill for making the posseseion of a certificate of competency compulsory in the case of enginemen on land, as is the case in the marine ser- vice ? s,—Are you in favour of an alteration of the law I relating to coroners' inquests which will give the right to relatives of deceased workmen to be represented at such inquiries ? Mr. Mospratt's reply is as follows :—" Liverpool, Novem- ber 6th,1885. Sir,—ln reply to your circular asking me my views oiacertain questions affecting railway servants, I think on referring to my speech at Widnes on Tut sday, you will find that I specially referred to Mr. Burt's amended Employer's Liability Bill with approval. I am, so far as I understand them, in accord with your seciety on the other ma ters referred to in your circular. No body of men can know so well as railway servants themselves what protec- tion they require.—Assuring you of my general sympathy with you in your endeavouring to improve your position, I remain, yours faithfully, E. K. MUSPRATT." . Mr. T. C. Moss, the Conservative candidate, has not yet replied. MR. MOSS AND THE PUBLICANS. A deputation trom the Widnes District Licensed Victual- lers' Association, consisting of Messrs. Hargreaves, Chap- man, and Gerrard, waited on Mr. Thomas Cottinghatn Edwards Moss at the Committee-rooms, Victoria-road, for the purpose of ascertaining his views on a number of mat- ters connected with their trade. During the course of a lung conversation they put several questions to him. and Mr. Mess eaid that the matter would require very careful consideration, ami that he would give them his decision in the course of a few days. The deputation acknowledged themselves highly pleased with the interview.

"If you don't keep out of this yard you'll catch it !" said a woman to a boy in West Lynn. "All right," answered the gamin, "I wouldn't , have come in if I'd known your folks had it." A Sr. HELENS DOCTOR SENT TO AN ASYLNIS. —At St. Helens Police Court en Monday morning, before Mr. Wm. Blinkhorn and Alderman Harrison, Mr. Stewart, relieving afficer for the Prescot Union, made an applicatibn for the committal of Mr. Bernard L. Hifferman, surgeon. to an asylum as being a person of unsound mind. It will be re- membered that on Wednesday last Dr. Hifferman was plain- tiff in an action arising out of a dispute which he bad with Mr. Wilson, of Hall-street, and a verdict was given in favour of Hifferman. In the County Court it was evident that Hifferman was under the influence of drink, and since that day he has been drinking heavily. On Friday morning he presented himself at the police office, and said that at mid- night six melt, with blackened faces, had entered his surgery and attacked him in a brutal manner. He knocked four of them down, and the others escaped after breaking his "wrist, which he had bandaged up. On Monday morning be went again to the police office and said be had been attacked by twenty men, but he knocked them all down. It was at once apparent that Dr. Hifferman was not in his right mind, and while be remained at the office he made other state- ments which confirmed that view. He said if he had a re- volver be would shoot certain people. Dr. McNicoll made an examination of Hifferman, and certified that he was of unsound mind. While In court Hifferman jumped up suddenly and rushed to the door, but was brought back by several officers, and when called upon to stand before the bench he commenced crying bitterly'. After inspecting the necessary forms which bad been filled, the magistrates made an order for his removal to Rainhill County Asylum, to which place he was conveyed the same day.

Considerable uproar fol- lowed. There were cries of "Turn him out," mingled with cheers and slight hisses. Mr. R. H. Wright ultimately made his way to the platform where he took a seat amid slight cheers and groans. Mr. Luffman then proceeded with his address. The Chairman then informed Mr. Wright that he was at liberty to say a few words if he wished. Mr. Wright was received with hisses and cheers. He briefly said he wished to repeat an assertion he had made In the body of the room that Sir Richard Cross's address was food for men and not for. babes. (Hisses and Cheers.) Mr. John Crosfield, J.P., of Warrrington, then addressed the meeting it some length. He urged that the Liberal party had had to fight hard to regain the libeities of the people, and said it was a piece of monstrous audacity ter the Tories to say that they passed the last reform bill. (Cheers.) They did nothing of the sort, and if they had the power—if his friends Sir Gilbert Greene!! and Sir Richard Cross—(hisses)—had the power—and if they dared, they would take away the vote from them to-morrow. Dresser (Liverpool). and carried amid cheers again and again renewed. Twenty or thirty hands were held up against the motion. A vote of thanks to the chairman then concluded the meeting.
